sources.title: How Roman got 11M Reddit impressions and $30K MRR for Gojiberry AI
sources.originalTitle: How I Used Reddit to Build a $34K/Month SaaS
sources.summary: Roman, co-founder of Gojiberry AI, explains the Reddit system that drove 11M+ impressions and 40K+ site visitors, taking his SaaS from zero to ~$30K MRR in months. He covers account warm-up, story-led posts with proof, coordinated early upvotes, and handling negativity.

principles.text: Write story posts with proof and keep your product out of the post body; spark curiosity instead.
principles.quote: never putting your SAS directly in the post. You can trigger curiosity by highlighting it. And as I said before, putting some proof and the people reading this post know that it's real

principles.text: Turn any life or business event, even a failure, into a Reddit story; you don't need big success to share.
principles.quote: you can turn any event happening in your life into a Reddit post.

principles.text: Warm up a fresh account for 7 to 14 days with comments and upvotes before any marketing.
principles.quote: for the first 7 to 14 days, don't even think of doing marketing. You will just post comments. You will upvote.

principles.text: Secure early upvotes: a group of marketers upvote and comment on each other's posts in the first minutes.
principles.quote: you need at least 10 up votes in the first 10 minutes.

principles.text: Reply to every comment to build engagement, which lifts upvotes and ranking.
principles.quote: you reply to every comment, absolutely every one of them. This is going to give you traction.

principles.text: Handle haters with proof, blocking, and conviction; negativity at the start is normal.
principles.quote: you show that you make it. So that's really easy and then you block all the people insulting you or being really negative

sources.title: How Romàn Czerny used cold email to book demos and grow Goji Berry to $2.5M
sources.originalTitle: How He Built a $2.5M Company With Cold Email
sources.summary: Romàn explains his cold email playbook: validate the market by booking demos before building, then turn outbound into inbound by offering a blueprint instead of asking for a call. He covers lead quality, volume, deliverability rules and why 1% reply rates still pay off.

principles.text: Use cold email to test the market and book demos before you build the product.
principles.quote: the goal here is to book as many demos as you can before building the product. So you can talk to your core audience. You try to sell them something and if they agree or if they ask okay what's the price then there might be something to do

sources.title: How GojiBerry went from $50k to $300k MRR by stacking and rotating distribution channels
sources.originalTitle: I make $3.5M/year with a LinkedIn AI Agent
sources.summary: Romàn Czerny explains how GojiBerry scaled by adding a new channel at each stage (outbound, Reddit, content, then YC, X, paid influencers, affiliates and UGC) and cutting low-return ones. He covers delegating proven channels to agencies, targeting the broader AI niche for reach, and what Y Combinator actually provided.

principles.text: Switch to a new revenue channel once you've mastered the current one or hit its ceiling.
principles.quote: at every different stage of your SaaS, you need a different revenue channel, I think. So, the philosophy we have is always to go to another channel once we have mastered one or once we feel that we cannot do more on one channel.

principles.text: Cut channels by opportunity cost: drop one when the same time earns far more elsewhere.
principles.quote: And if we take that time and put it into B2B influencers, UGCs, any other channel, we get way more.

principles.text: Test a channel yourself first, then hand your proven blueprint to an agency.
principles.quote: every time I want to add a channel, I test it myself and then I delegate to an agency.

principles.text: Aim your content at the broader, hotter AI niche rather than your narrow category to multiply reach (churn tradeoff).
principles.quote: If you do blueprints about AI, um the distribution is going to 10x.

principles.text: Buy viral launches on X by paying people who quote-retweet comparable SaaS launches.
principles.quote: If you look at the biggest launch from XField or or even anything which is a a SaaS, you can look at who is quote retweeting the tweet. You DM those people.

principles.text: Founder-led content can't be fully outsourced; use agencies for angles and rework the output.
principles.quote: Because it is founder-led content, it's very hard for an agency to know what's happening inside the brain of a founder.

sources.title: How Roman sold before building and took Goji Berry to $33K+ MRR through relentless outreach
sources.originalTitle: I Built 2 SaaS Apps to $50K MRR: Here's My 90-Day Playbook
sources.summary: Roman explains why his first SaaS failed (no customer talks), how a cloned Shopify app reached $500K/yr and sold, and how he pre-sold a lead service before coding Goji Berry. Covers his cold outreach stack, blueprint offer, multi-channel distribution and a 90-day plan for new B2B founders.

principles.text: Start from the customer: how badly they want the problem solved and what they'll pay.
principles.quote: Everything starts with the customer, not with the product. How much do they want to solve this problem and how much are they willing to pay?

principles.text: Get paid before you code; money upfront is the strongest validation.
principles.quote: having money before you code is a great great sign. It means that really you you are into something.

principles.text: Outreach is the best first channel because it gives instant, scalable feedback on your offer.
principles.quote: When you send 5,000 emails, if you don't get any answers, well, you know, your offer is not good or your messaging is not good.

principles.text: Offer a free blueprint instead of asking for a demo; it's an easier yes.
principles.quote: saying yes to a blueprint is way easier than saying yes for a demo.

principles.text: Email customer service with a demo video and ask them to forward it to the CEO; it avoids spam and gets replies.
principles.quote: instead of emailing the founder, we would email the customer service with um a demo video and ask the customer service to forward it to the CEO and they would almost always do it.

principles.text: Add distribution channels one at a time, learning each, rather than picking just one or two.
principles.quote: my process is posting a lot on one channel, understanding how it works and then adding more and more channels every day.

sources.title: Romàn Czerny: copying proven SaaS, pre-selling before coding, and exiting Cocoai for $1M+
sources.originalTitle: 3 Idées de SaaS à +1M€ à lancer
sources.summary: Romàn Czerny recounts selling his WhatsApp e-commerce SaaS Cocoai (about $50k MRR, sold for over $1M) and killing two failed ideas before finding Gojiberry, a buying-signal tool. He explains how he validates by pre-selling, why he copies proven products, and where he sees SaaS opportunities in sales tooling and US micro-niches.

principles.text: Pre-sell with a landing page and never write code before someone pays.
principles.quote: je coderais pas une seule ligne avant qu'on me donne de l'argent.

principles.text: Build for the most pressing need every business has: getting more customers.
principles.quote: c'est quoi le le besoin le plus pressant de de tous les gens à qui on a parlé depuis le début ? Et c'est en fait c'est avoir plus de clients.

principles.text: Copy what already works, then add your own twist or advantage.
principles.quote: vraiment regarder ce qui fonctionne et voir un petit peu où est-ce où est-ce que où est-ce que tu peux rajouter ton ton grain de sel.

principles.text: Niche down in big markets like the US to reach one target and build a network.
principles.quote: en nichahant, tu vas tu vas pouvoir parler directement à une cible.

principles.text: Platform dependency is a real risk and can justify selling the business.
principles.quote: WhatsApp c'est dépendant de MTA et Meta change ses règles tous les 3 mois de manière totalement arbitraire.

principles.text: Take a tech cofounder instead of paying a dev, and keep a cash cushion before starting SaaS.
principles.quote: prenez toujours un cfounder tech euh parce que si vous payez un dev, ça va coûter très cher

sources.title: How Gojiberry AI hit $2M ARR: validate by hand, then scale warm-intent outreach
sources.originalTitle: How Gojiberry AI Hit $2M ARR With Cold Outreach That Actually Works
sources.summary: Roman, co-founder and CMO of Gojiberry, explains how he validated the product by manually finding leads for paying customers before building. He covers outreach on intent signals instead of static databases, a Reddit-to-multichannel funnel, lead magnet and webinar distribution, and paywalling AI SaaS to control costs.

principles.text: Sell it manually before building. Real payment is the validation, not polite interest.
principles.quote: if people are not throwing their credit cards at you um then you don't have the right products.

principles.text: Start with outbound calls and volume to learn who buys and why; skip social media for the first 10 to 50 customers.
principles.quote: I would never start a SAS without uh doing calls at the beginning. Even if it's painful, you need those calls.

principles.text: Target leads showing intent today, not stale database contacts, to get 2 to 5x more replies.
principles.quote: we get two to five times more reply than our competitors that are using um static databases just because we are looking for leads that are warm um today

principles.text: Make the cold reply effortless: a low-effort yes beats a question that needs thought.
principles.quote: I've done X for Y, I can show you how. Reply yes and I'll send it to you.

principles.text: Use one channel as a cheap validation funnel (Reddit), learn who converts, then expand to X, LinkedIn and cold email.
principles.quote: Reddit was my my validation. Um, I think we went from zero to 20K MR just with Reddit.

principles.text: Put a paywall on AI SaaS from day one, since free usage costs tokens and attracts users who can't pay.
principles.quote: at the beginning when you sign up there is a pay wall. You need to put your credit card um and then get access to 7-day free trial.

sources.title: How Goji Berry books demos: intent signals, blueprint lead magnets and competitor-review YouTube SEO
sources.originalTitle: How to Use AI to Find and Convert High-Intent Leads on LinkedIn
sources.summary: Román Czerny, co-founder of Goji Berry AI, explains how his team finds high-intent LinkedIn leads and turns them into meetings. He covers active-lead targeting, giving value before asking for a demo, lead-magnet distribution across channels, and funnel numbers (about 70% demo close, 35% trial to paid).

principles.text: Target people who were active on LinkedIn in the last 24 hours; it can at least double outreach results.
principles.quote: if you contact people who were posting on LinkedIn in the past 24 hours you will at least double your results so that's what we saw

principles.text: Don't push a demo after one or two messages. Offer a valuable blueprint first and let prospects book themselves.
principles.quote: if you try to book a demo with someone after one or two message, that's a bit aggressive. People are fed up.

principles.text: Make the lead magnet the core marketing asset and obsess over improving and distributing it.
principles.quote: my goal as a marketer is to create the best lead magnet.

principles.text: Combine job title and location with what the lead is talking about or interacting with, not just firmographics.
principles.quote: You don't do it based on job title plus location plus knowing what the lead is talking about or interacting about.

principles.text: Publish review videos of competitors with a pitch for your alternative; they rank for high-intent searches.
principles.quote: So what we've been doing on YouTube is take all our competitors and make reviews about them.

principles.text: Use AI for sourcing and drafting, but have a human take over once a prospect replies to book the demo.
principles.quote: If you put AI end to end, you get way fewer demo than if when the prospect respond, you take over and you try to to book the demo.

sources.title: How Gojiberry's founder gets 50% LinkedIn reply rates with intent signals and a lead-magnet ask
sources.originalTitle: 3x Your LinkedIn Reply Rate ft. Gojiberry AI
sources.summary: Roman explains why LinkedIn outreach should target only high-intent leads (right ICP, recently active, showing a signal) instead of sending more volume. He walks through signal and lookalike agents, how to prune weak keywords, and the low-friction "can I send you a blueprint?" message that drives his best demo flow.

principles.text: With limited LinkedIn invites, win by quality: reach only high-intent leads rather than sending more volume.
principles.quote: Especially on LinkedIn since you can only reach out to 200 um connections per week then you maximize the return you have on those 200 uh weekly connections.

principles.text: Intent means right ICP plus recent activity plus a signal; even mere recent activity roughly doubles response.
principles.quote: Probably the lowest one would be um active on LinkedIn in the past 48 hours, which means it still doubles your um response when you reach out to these people

principles.text: Start broad on signals, then prune: check which keywords produce demos and replace dead ones.
principles.quote: You look at where they come from. So you say, okay, that keyword is really strong. That keyword is really weak. I got no demos out of it. So you delete that keyword, you replace it with another one.

principles.text: Split agents by warmth (competitor-aware vs. engaged with you) into separate campaigns so you can measure each.
principles.quote: I separated the two um so I could create separate campaigns one for each um and really dissociate uh within like really dissociate solution aware and people that interacted with me or my team

principles.text: Ask permission to send a lead magnet. Make replying require almost no thought, with a high cost of missing out.
principles.quote: When you are looking for replies uh you want the lead to think as little as possible.

principles.text: Your LinkedIn profile is a proof-of-identity sales page, and a thin profile tanks acceptance rates.
principles.quote: I see some people coming into goji berry they have a LinkedIn account without any picture without any banners without any job experience and they see a poor acceptance rate.

sources.title: How GojiBerry hit $1M ARR in 9 months with a multi-channel growth engine
sources.originalTitle: If you're starting a SaaS in 2026, do this (how we hit $1M ARR in 9 months)
sources.summary: A full walkthrough of GojiBerry's go-to-market: validate with a few slides and calls, start with outbound, then layer inbound, paid, SEO and demos. The common thread is lead magnets and high-intent targeting across LinkedIn, cold email, X, Reddit, YouTube and influencers.

principles.text: Validate demand before coding: prove people will pay by presenting to your ICP.
principles.quote: before coding, before doing anything, you need to know if some persons if some people are willing to pay for what you are doing.

principles.text: With no customers yet, start with outbound to get fast feedback, then add inbound, paid and SEO.
principles.quote: if you do not have any clients, outbound is the best way to go. You need results fast.

principles.text: Target leads who just showed intent instead of static job-title lists; it multiplies replies.
principles.quote: When you do high intent lead outreach, well, it's very simple. You get three five times more responses than doing ICP based outreach.

principles.text: Copy lead magnets the market already demands and send them via cold email and content.
principles.quote: always go on LinkedIn and see what are the best lead magnets on my market. Lead magnets I know people want because they ask for it on LinkedIn.

principles.text: On Reddit, tell stories with proof instead of promoting; entertainment earns attention.
principles.quote: if you try to promote, it's not going to work. You always need to entertain people.

principles.text: Use B2B influencers only for viral lead-magnet posts, paid after the post goes live.
principles.quote: my goal is to do viral posts. Only viral posts. No videos, no points of views, nothing.

sources.title: How Gojiberry hit $3.2M ARR: manual sales, Reddit, LinkedIn lead magnets, influencers, YC
sources.originalTitle: He built a SaaS so good that YC was FORCED to accept him
sources.summary: Romàn Czerny, CMO of Gojiberry, walks through each growth phase from 0 to $3.2M ARR: selling manually before building, spamming Reddit, then industrializing LinkedIn lead magnets and paid B2B influencers. He also covers card-required trials, ads economics and what YC changed.

principles.text: Sell the solution manually before coding it; validate demand with a crappy deck and hand-delivered results.
principles.quote: Now, sell the solution, and then as soon as you sell it, we start coding it.

principles.text: Each growth phase needs its own channel: outreach, then Reddit, then LinkedIn lead magnets, then influencers and ads.
principles.quote: each phase had its own channel, I would say.

principles.text: If starting from scratch, do outreach first: you can launch in two days and it tests your offer fast.
principles.quote: if I had to start a business from scratch, I would do outreach because the thing is that you can launch in 2 days maximum, and it allows you to test your offer very easily.

principles.text: Require a card on free trials: it filters abusers and unserious users, and lifts trial-to-paid conversion.
principles.quote: the card is important. With the card, it's super important for a lot of reasons.

principles.text: In a red ocean, being seen more than competitors wins the market, so pair visibility with one differentiating angle.
principles.quote: on the red oceans, uh, well in fact, if it's a red ocean, it means that there is business, and if there is business, if you are seen, well you simply take the business.

principles.text: Lead magnets ending in a sales page scale linearly; B2B LinkedIn influencers are underpriced, so buy proven posts.
principles.quote: there are very few companies that pay influencers on LinkedIn, which makes it really easy to find deals.

sources.title: How Romàn Czerny built Ecom French Touch: cheap high-recurrence products and a 25k Facebook community
sources.originalTitle: De 0 à +100k abonnés jusqu'à travailler avec Djibril Cissé ? - avec Roman Czerny (Ecom French Touch)
sources.summary: Romàn Czerny explains why Ecom French Touch sells low-priced, frequently repurchased info products backed by proof of its own results. He covers how the team grew a 25k-member Facebook group, then moved the audience to YouTube and Telegram, and what the PayPal freeze taught him about diversifying.

principles.text: Sell low-priced products with high repurchase frequency to rebuild trust in a burned market.
principles.quote: by offering prices that are very low but with a high purchase recurrence, we actually restored confidence in these people who buy online training

principles.text: Sell on provable results of your own; everything you sell should be demonstrable.
principles.quote: we can prove it 100% and people know it

principles.text: A big audience only sticks if you give it a lot of value; community management is what retains people.
principles.quote: what worked is that we also gave these people an enormous amount of value

principles.text: Pour all your audience into one platform first, then transfer it to others once you have a base.
principles.quote: pick one platform to blow up, so you really drain all the audience you can onto that platform

principles.text: Focus on the platform that matches your zone of genius, where you are strong and enjoy it.
principles.quote: focus on a platform where you are close to your zone of genius, that's super important

principles.text: Always diversify networks, payment processors and tools, after a PayPal freeze blocked a big chunk of revenue.
principles.quote: that you must always diversify, whether it's networks, payment processors, or page systems

sources.title: How Romàn reached €20k MRR with Gojiberry AI: validation, pricing, and intent-led outbound
sources.originalTitle: How to reach 20k MRR for your SaaS (Romàn's guide)
sources.summary: Romàn's playbook from scaling two SaaS (Coco AI to €500k ARR, now Gojiberry AI): validate with real conversations before coding, build one feature, match competitor pricing, and win the first 10 customers manually. Growth then comes from high-intent LinkedIn outreach, Reddit, cold email on fresh signals, and cheap compounding channels like free tools, blog, directories and YouTube.

principles.text: Validate by getting people ready to pay before writing code; talk to prospects and pivot fast.
principles.quote: That’s the most important signal: if people are ready to give you their credit card before you’ve written a single line of code, you’re on the right track.

principles.text: Build one feature only, and only if it lifts retention, customer results, or revenue.
principles.quote: Never build a feature unless you are 100% sure it will either increase retention, improve your customer’s results, or grow your revenue. Everything else is a waste of time.

principles.text: Start pricing by matching competitors who are already selling, then test and adjust based on churn and sales effort.
principles.quote: I start by matching the competition, because if they’re winning at that price, there’s no reason my offer can’t perform just as well.

principles.text: Grind manually for the first 10 customers: get 20-30 meetings, close 10, and don't accept 'maybe later'.
principles.quote: The goal is simple: get 20 to 30 meetings and close ten of them. At this stage, it’s all about taking action.

principles.text: Target high-intent leads showing real-time signals instead of cold lists; timing beats volume.
principles.quote: Think less about cold lists and more about real-time triggers

principles.text: Cold email fails mostly from stale lead sources, so email fresh intent signals rather than static databases.
principles.quote: The #1 reason cold email fails isn’t copy or deliverability. It’s lead source.

sources.title: Reddit Strategy Playbook: How Gojiberry gets 30% of demos from Reddit without getting banned
sources.summary: Romàn Czerny, co-founder of gojiberry.ai, lays out the Reddit system that brings him 30% of his demos. It covers picking subreddits, commenting without getting banned, measuring results with short sprints, and the post formats that work. It also explains how Reddit threads feed Google and LLM visibility.

principles.text: Give more than you take on Reddit; only mention your product when it is the natural solution.
principles.quote: Always prioritize helping others. Read the user’s problem, give advice, and only mention your product when it’s the natural, relevant solution.

principles.text: Treat links as a risk: name your product, and share a link only when someone asks.
principles.quote: Mention your product by name (people will Google it if they’re curious).

principles.text: Warm up a new account with genuine contributions before promoting, then scale mentions gradually.
principles.quote: Don’t promote on a cold account. Get at least 10 karma before mentioning your SaaS

principles.text: Measure Reddit with short intensive sprints followed by pauses, then compare subreddit groups by sign-ups.
principles.quote: Post around 20 relevant mentions per day for 3 days to trigger a visible traffic spike.

principles.text: Reddit is an SEO and AI-visibility channel: threads get cited by Google and LLMs, so mentions compound over time.
principles.quote: Reddit is one of the most cited sources in LLMs like ChatGPT. In fact, around 40% of AI-generated answers reference Reddit.

principles.text: Use a repeatable post mix and target threads that already rank on Google for free compounding exposure.
principles.quote: Threads that already rank for years = free compounding exposure.

sources.title: Claude for Small Business: why prospecting is the sales gap AI back-office tools leave open
sources.originalTitle: Claude for Small Business: The Sales Pipeline Gap Anthropic Didn't Touch
sources.summary: Gojiberry's essay argues Anthropic's Claude for Small Business automates back-office work on data that already exists, but leaves top-of-funnel prospecting untouched. It frames sales as two columns (before and after a lead lands in the CRM) and says the moat is moving upstream. It is also a product pitch for Gojiberry.

principles.text: Managing existing demand is different from creating new demand; AI ops tools only do the first.
principles.quote: managing demand ≠ creating demand

principles.text: Build prospecting first, not last; deferring it makes it the bottleneck.
principles.quote: Most small teams build their stack in the wrong order: CRM first, then sequencing tool, then "we'll figure out prospecting later." But "later" is the bottleneck.

principles.text: As post-lead workflows get automated, the competitive moat moves up the funnel to sourcing leads.
principles.quote: If your post-lead workflow is about to get automated for free with Claude, your competitive moat moves up the funnel.

principles.text: Horizontal AI agents orchestrate existing data; they don't go find new prospects.
principles.quote: Claude orchestrates what's there. It doesn't go fetch what isn't.

principles.text: Prospecting is its own vertical needing specialized tooling, not a feature bolted onto a general agent.
principles.quote: Sales prospecting is a vertical with its own data plumbing, scoring logic, and intent signals.

principles.text: Keep a human checkpoint before outbound goes out; full automation without one is a red flag.
principles.quote: If a sales AI vendor pitches you full automation with no human checkpoint before outbound goes out, that's a red flag.

sources.title: B2B sales automation: what to automate first and what to keep manual
sources.originalTitle: B2B sales automation: how to automate your sales process in 2026
sources.summary: A small sales team should automate in a fixed order: logging, booking, follow-up timing, signal-based targeting, then drafting. Four jobs stay human: replies, objections, pricing, and anything a bad list would multiply. The essay also gives a deliverability checklist and a 4-week plan for a 3-person team.

principles.text: Automation multiplies what you feed it, so fix the list and process before scaling sends.
principles.quote: Automation multiplies whatever you feed it. Send a good sequence to the wrong list and you'll reach the wrong people faster, with better follow-up.

principles.text: Automate the safest, cheapest work first: logging activity into a CRM that no prospect ever sees.
principles.quote: Start here because it costs nothing and breaks nothing.

principles.text: Let software handle follow-up timing but write the messages yourself, since follow-ups are the first thing prospects notice.
principles.quote: Write them yourself and let the tool handle the timing.

principles.text: Never automate the reply to a real reply. Answer personally, fast, from your own mailbox.
principles.quote: Write back yourself, from your own mailbox, within the day.

principles.text: Build the follow-up and booking machinery before investing in better targeting, or good leads leak out.
principles.quote: Better targeting only pays once you can act on it.

principles.text: Consistency in touches beats a high touch count; the rule of 7 is folklore with a useful shape.
principles.quote: Three touches you send every time will beat seven you send when you remember.

sources.title: AI sales agents: autonomous vs assistive, real costs, and why per-team pricing wins for small teams
sources.originalTitle: AI sales agent: what they cost and which type you need
sources.summary: A buyer's guide that splits AI sales agents into autonomous (run the whole loop) and assistive (a rep still sends), then compares ten tools and their pricing models. Core lessons: pick the type before the tool, watch what the price meter counts (seat, team, credits), and lead outreach with a real signal rather than volume. It is a vendor post, so claims favor Gojiberry.

principles.text: Choose the agent type (autonomous vs assistive) before comparing tools; type matters more than rank.
principles.quote: Sorted into the two types rather than ranked one to ten, because the type decides far more than the ranking does.

principles.text: Check what the price meter counts. Per-seat pricing scales with headcount; flat team pricing doesn't.
principles.quote: A 49 dollar seat costs 147 a month for three reps and 490 for ten. A flat team price doesn't move.

principles.text: Autonomy without supervision or targeting creates volume, not pipeline.
principles.quote: An agent nobody supervises produces volume rather than pipeline.

principles.text: In outreach, the reason for writing beats the number of channels or messages.
principles.quote: The channel count matters less than the reason for writing, and it isn't close.

principles.text: The best prospects are often those with a recent trigger, not those already on a list.
principles.quote: the people who replied were never the ones on any list.

principles.text: Know where signal-based selling fails: markets whose buyers leave no online trace.
principles.quote: When your buyers leave no trace online, no signal engine invents activity that isn't there.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Roman, co-founder of Gojiberry AI, explains the Reddit system that drove 11M+ impressions and 40K+ site visitors, taking his SaaS from zero to ~$30K MRR in months. He covers account warm-up, story-led posts with proof, coordinated early upvotes, and handling negativity.

chunks.heading: Reddit as a first-100-customers channel: scale, results and why it works
chunks.text:
Romàn co-founded Gojiberry AI, an intent-based LinkedIn outreach SaaS. It was at $0 revenue about four months before the interview and was near $30K MRR (a dashboard showed about $24K MRR) by the time he spoke. Most users are on the $99 plan, which gives unlimited high-intent leads.

- Reddit was a main early acquisition channel. It produced "over 11 million" impressions and more than 40,000 website visitors.
- He says buying that reach would have cost "hundreds of thousands of dollars". It got the first roughly 100 customers.
- A hidden benefit: nearly every lead on a demo call or on another platform has already seen him on Reddit ("Oh, you are the Reddit guy"). He argues the more often a lead sees you, the more likely you close them on a call.
- His earlier SaaS, Coco AI, was scaled to $50K MRR with outreach and sold to a US venture. He credits the acquisition method for its success and built Gojiberry on the same logic.

chunks.heading: Post formula: story plus proof, with the product never pitched directly
chunks.text:
Romàn's best posts are stories with evidence, not ads.

- **"I paid 5 influencers on LinkedIn to promote my SaaS. Here's what $1,250 got me."** It got 160K views and 543 upvotes, about 2,000 site visitors, and roughly 10 to 15 clients. He included the influencer posts and all available proof.
- **A Y Combinator rejection post** (selected for the interview, failed it). It got more than 179,000 views and roughly 15 clients.
- Rules he follows:
  - Tell a story and show proof so readers know it is real.
  - Never put the SaaS directly in the post. Trigger curiosity so people look it up.
  - Any event in your life can become a post, including a failure.
- If you have no success to share yet, write about how the SaaS is going and what problem you are trying to solve. He says anyone can get views and traffic this way.
- Ideas come from his daily work as a SaaS marketer: the more he does, the more stories he has.

chunks.heading: Writing workflow with AI
chunks.text:
- Romàn is not a native English speaker. He tells the story to ChatGPT by voice, then has it translate and correct the text.
- He says speaking lets him go into far more detail than typing everything out.
- He uses ChatGPT plus Nano Banana for every post and graphic. This costs about $40/month.

chunks.heading: Account setup and warm-up playbook
chunks.text:
1. Use a fresh account per browser. He runs one each on Chrome, Firefox and Safari, which he calls "more than enough to keep it safe".
2. Do not create the Reddit account with a brand-new email. He says new email plus new Reddit account gets you banned right away.
3. Add a profile picture, link the SaaS in the bio, and turn on the setting that hides your feed. Otherwise people who open your profile see you always talking about the same SaaS and conclude you advertise too much.
4. For the first 7 to 14 days do no marketing. Only comment and upvote to warm up the account and earn first karma. More karma means a stronger account.
5. After 7 to 14 days, start posting, then start marketing.
6. Skip subreddits that ban promotion or are moderated so tightly that posting is almost impossible.
7. Change the angle on every post. You can redirect to a YouTube video or a Twitter post, which he calls "the magic of Reddit".

chunks.heading: Getting a post seen: early upvotes and engagement
chunks.text:
- Target at least 10 upvotes in the first 10 minutes (elsewhere he says as many as possible in the first 5 to 10 minutes).
- He has a group of friends who share each other's posts and upvote and comment on each one. Internally this is a group of 15 marketers. Early momentum then pushes the post to external users and ranks it higher.
- Reply to every single comment. This shows engagement, which brings more upvotes and a higher rank.

chunks.heading: Handling negativity and bans
chunks.text:
- Show proof so no one can argue with you. For example, if you make $25K MRR, show it.
- Block people who insult you or are purely negative.
- He says it can be frightening at first, since a post can draw 15 bad comments saying you will never make it. You have to stick with it and believe in what you are doing.

chunks.heading: Gojiberry's marketing stack and costs
chunks.text:
- Instantly AI for cold email: about $800/month, because of very high volume.
- Outrank for SEO: about $99/month.
- Gojiberry AI itself for LinkedIn and high-intent outreach: about $99/month.
- Cal.com-style booking tool for calls: about $20/month.
- Framer for the website and landing pages: about $49/month.
- ChatGPT plus Nano Banana for post and graphic creation: about $40/month.
- LinkedIn Sales Navigator on some accounts: about $100/month.

chunks.heading: Product and positioning
chunks.text:
- Gojiberry finds high-intent leads on LinkedIn from signals: someone liking a specific post, engaging with a competitor, or having just raised funds or hired.
- Each day it surfaces the warmest leads, and users launch campaigns from the same tool. It automates connection requests and AI-personalized messages.
- Romàn says acceptance and reply rates are well above industry norms because the leads are strong and the messaging is tailored per lead.

chunks.heading: Core advice
chunks.text: - "Advertise the way you would love to be advertised to." He likes founder stories like Starter Story's, because hearing how someone succeeded makes him want to learn more, and he markets the same way.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn explains his cold email playbook: validate the market by booking demos before building, then turn outbound into inbound by offering a blueprint instead of asking for a call. He covers lead quality, volume, deliverability rules and why 1% reply rates still pay off.

chunks.heading: Why Romàn uses cold email to start a B2B business
chunks.text:
- Romàn calls cold email his favorite way to start a B2B business. It lets him test the market without launching on social media, which he says is a lot of work and hard to pivot on every two weeks.
- His approach is to email and LinkedIn-outreach a bunch of people and book as many demos as possible before building the product.
- At Goji Berry (high-intent lead finding and outreach software), the first customers were sold lead files before the product existed. He did the work manually, which took the company from zero to 10K.
- He stopped the manual work once he knew he was onto something, knew who to sell to and how to sell it, and then built the software.
- He says the same playbook helped grow his previous SaaS, Coco AI.
- Goji Berry is at roughly €2.5M a year. He estimates cold email plus LinkedIn outreach drove about 30% of the first year's revenue.
- His view: cold email is "way easier than getting viral on X, way easier than getting viral on LinkedIn, way easier than making a YouTube video."
- He compares the cold-email-versus-no-cold-email debate to bootstrapped-versus-VC-backed: people love taking sides, but both can work.

chunks.heading: The three ingredients of cold email
chunks.text:
- Romàn says you need three things: a targeted lead list with real emails in your ICP, the infrastructure, and the right messaging.
- He argues people over-focus on infrastructure, such as spam and domains. In his view the hardest part is getting demos, meaning the messaging and offer.
- Cold emailing is legal if you:
  - let people unsubscribe,
  - stop when asked,
  - send something related to their business that helps them grow.
- First step for a beginner: set up infrastructure, get leads (high-intent, scraped, or from a database like Apollo), enrich the emails, write the messaging, then launch.
- Budget: be ready to spend about $100 to $500 to try it.
- Small volume: 1,000 to 2,000 emails a month is "more than enough" to start, and needs only two or three mailboxes.

chunks.heading: Infrastructure setup and volume rules
chunks.text:
- Romàn used Instantly in the early days. He added new mailboxes, used done-for-you email setup, or bought pre-warmed accounts. He spent roughly $500 to $800 a month on Instantly. He was moving off it to Goji Berry's own email infrastructure, which now has email steps in multi-channel campaigns.
- Goji Berry lets you send email, but you bring your own domains. Instantly lets you buy domains.
- Deliverability rules he follows:
  - No links in the original message.
  - Avoid spam words, such as 18+ content, money, gambling and drugs, and "promotion" or "promo code".
  - Send a maximum of 30 emails per mailbox per day.
  - Use three mailboxes per domain.
  - Spin the email so a word changes per recipient (Instantly does this almost automatically), or use Goji Berry personalization per lead.
- He says spam placement mostly comes from irrelevant offers that nobody replies to. When recipients reply and engage, Gmail and Outlook see healthy conversations.
- Mailboxes eventually land in spam, so he expects to rotate them regularly.

chunks.heading: The blueprint offer: give before you ask
chunks.text:
- Romàn calls asking for a demo in the first email the biggest cold email mistake. You are asking a stranger for their time before giving anything.
- Instead, he offers a "blueprint" (a free guide). The recipient replies "yes", which is low effort compared with agreeing to a meeting.
- His example email goes to people who commented on his LinkedIn post. It says they commented to get the "cloud power prospecting system", described as the exact setup used to book 100+ meetings in a few weeks. It then asks if they received it and says to reply "yes" to have it resent.
- After the reply, he sends a document containing:
  - a video,
  - another video,
  - a full playbook on getting leads,
  - at the bottom, a link to start a trial or book a demo.
- This turns outbound into inbound. People who book have read the document and chosen to book, so they show up wanting to buy.
- He says that since discovering this, he has "never asked for a demo in cold email ever again."
- The same pattern works with other assets:
  - a YouTube video ("I broke down in a video how we did X for Y, can I send it?"),
  - a free tool,
  - a Slack group.
- He claims you could get around 1,000 people a month watching a video this way.
- Cold email at volume also drives traffic to your site and works as retargeting, because recipients then see you on X, LinkedIn and ads.

chunks.heading: Lead sourcing
chunks.text:
- Romàn has two ways of getting leads:
  - Scraping a high volume of leads, enriching them, and uploading them to Instantly.
  - High-intent leads generated by Goji Berry, sent with more context and personalization. Volume is lower but response rates are far higher.
- Goji Berry's high-intent signals:
  - engaged with a competitor,
  - liked LinkedIn posts with specific keywords,
  - similar to the ideal lead and active.
- Goji's extension also pulls leads from Sales Navigator, search results, or the likers and commenters of any LinkedIn post. He then enriches the emails and sends via Goji or Instantly.

chunks.heading: Reply rates, volume and iteration
chunks.text:
- Romàn's numbers from an Instantly campaign:
  - Last 7 days: about 25K emails sent, reply rate roughly 1.19% including auto-replies.
  - One month: around 549 people replied, with an 84K-email campaign producing over 10 replies per day.
  - He says he probably sent more than 1 million emails in the last 12 months across campaigns.
- His view: 1% looks low, but at volume it is hard to do much better. He cites Adam Robinson of RB2B sending millions of emails a month at a 0.7 to 0.8% reply rate, and calls that "insane" given the cost.
- He suggests studying Robinson's approach: it pushes the free trial rather than demos.
- How he tests:
  - He doesn't run a split test. He finds a winning blueprint, goes all in until he has emailed everyone he can, then changes the blueprint and emails everyone again.
  - He sends few follow-ups, and sometimes just a second email with a different blueprint.
  - His rule: it is better to cold email someone new than to follow up on someone who hasn't responded. The exception is account-based marketing with big deals, where follow-ups are worth it.
- He says you never really run out of leads because you can always try a new angle. When he does, it's usually because he was busy with other channels.
- He copies and tests winning templates that others share publicly.

chunks.heading: Demos vs free trials, and when cold email fits
chunks.text:
- Romàn is trying to avoid demos. The demo link sits at the bottom of the document, and most people just take the free trial.
- Routing for people who do book:
  - Individuals and small teams go to a webinar (he runs three per week).
  - Teams of two to three go to someone else.
  - Teams above three get a meeting with him.
- When to use cold email:
  - It fits a B2B SaaS selling for roughly $100, $200 or $500 a month.
  - For $20 to $30 a month products, it is useful for getting on calls and learning what customers want, but not for making money.
- If you already have an audience, he would first test blueprints on it. Once one sticks, he would start cold email.
- If you have no audience, cold email lets you talk to customers and learn what they want without posting on social media.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn Czerny explains how GojiBerry scaled by adding a new channel at each stage (outbound, Reddit, content, then YC, X, paid influencers, affiliates and UGC) and cutting low-return ones. He covers delegating proven channels to agencies, targeting the broader AI niche for reach, and what Y Combinator actually provided.

chunks.heading: Distribution philosophy: one channel per revenue stage
chunks.text:
- Romàn argues that each stage of a SaaS needs a different revenue channel. GojiBerry's rule: move to a new channel once you have mastered one or cannot get more out of it.
- GojiBerry's path by MRR:
  - $0 to $6k: only outbound.
  - $10k to $25k: almost only Reddit.
  - $25k to $75k: content plus blueprints (free lead magnets).
  - $75k to ~$150k: Y Combinator exposure, X (Twitter), B2B influencers, sponsored newsletters and a lifetime affiliate program.
  - Later: UGC, Meta ads and viral X launches (see the paid-playbook section).
- Channels are added on top of each other. Romàn only cut one, Reddit, after about $250k MRR.
- He cut Reddit for two reasons:
  - Hate towards tool promotion ("I think we went a bit too hard").
  - Opportunity cost. A few $K of MRR from Reddit takes a lot of time, and the same time in B2B influencers or UGC returns more. Other people now talk about GojiBerry on Reddit without GojiBerry posting.
- He reached $300k MRR with GojiBerry. The company turned 1 year old days before the recording.

chunks.heading: Test a channel yourself, then hand it to an agency
chunks.text:
- Romàn does not hire much on the growth side. He handles growth himself and uses the best agency in each domain:
  - Agencies for B2B influencers, SEO, UGC, Meta ads and content.
  - Cold outreach is run in-house by an intern.
- The workflow:
  1. He tests each new channel himself.
  2. He writes his own blueprint of what works.
  3. He delegates to an agency that must follow that blueprint ("I know exactly what I want").
- Agencies cost money, but the cost is acceptable because he knows exactly what he wants.
- Next step: an in-house growth hire who takes his spot and manages agencies while he tests new channels.
- On X, he did everything himself at first. Now an agency suggests posts. He rejects most, but uses the hooks or angles as raw material and rewrites them.
- Founder-led content always needs rework because an agency cannot know what is in a founder's head.

chunks.heading: X and founder accounts
chunks.text:
- GojiBerry opened X accounts for all three founders. Romàn manages content for all of them.
- Before, they only posted on their own account. Paying B2B influencers to post lead magnets expanded the reach.
- The YC logo or "in YC" in a post brought a lot of exposure from the startup world, plus credibility.

chunks.heading: The paid and viral playbook (UGC, B2B creators, quote retweets)
chunks.text:
- Romàn follows a blueprint he attributes to companies such as XField, Arcads and Lovable.
- Steps:
  - **Organic to paid:** create content on TikTok and Instagram. When a piece goes viral, boost it with Meta/Instagram ads.
  - **LinkedIn:** pay B2B influencers to give away lead magnets about your brand.
  - **X viral launches:** look at who quote-retweeted the biggest SaaS launches. DM them and pay them to quote-retweet your tweet.
- The quote-retweet tactic: he had just started it. Per Romàn, $1,000 to $3,000 can buy a viral video on X that brings a lot of revenue.
- His forward plan is to focus on these three channels (UGC, B2B creators, quote retweets), raise the volume, and aim for $500k to $1M per month.
- Trade-off: this content attracts mostly individual users, small sales teams and small agencies, so retention is lower and going upmarket is harder.
- Romàn's answer to the churn: go all in on the channels. Heavy growth generates enough volume that the teams worth keeping consolidate from it. He also plans to bring in bigger teams.

chunks.heading: Target the AI niche, not your literal category
chunks.text:
- Biggest growth lever, per Romàn: free blueprints (lead-magnet content) aimed at the AI niche.
- His logic, using SEO as the example:
  - "How to improve SEO" targets a niche everyone already targets.
  - "How to improve your SEO with AI" reaches a bigger, newer audience. Claude puts out large budgets and creators get more reach talking about AI than SEO.
- GojiBerry's version: instead of "how to get more leads", it publishes content on how Claude, LLMs and ChatGPT get you better leads.
- This brings in people from AI and from outreach, not just the narrow category. He says distribution can go "10x".
- Trade-off: the niche is broader, so churn is higher.
- He says he would not change this move. GojiBerry's landing page also pitches an AI agent.
- He could not say how much the headline change lifted conversion. Traffic sources changed at the same time and tracking was not in place ("that's my fault"). He only knows the landing page converts well.
- He cautions that this will not fit every SaaS. He says to take what you can reproduce, not copy everything. He cites other founders' blueprints that may suit some products better.

chunks.heading: What Y Combinator gave GojiBerry
chunks.text:
- Process: three months in San Francisco. You need a US company to receive YC's money.
- Perks on day one included:
  - Almost $1M in OpenAI tokens.
  - $300k from Gemini and $300k from Claude.
  - Credits from AWS and Azure and other tools.
- Cost saving: for an AI tool these are costs you do not have to pay.
- Rhythm:
  - One conference per week.
  - One meeting per week with your assigned partner.
  - A group talk every two weeks with other founders.
  - Mostly working in a room with co-founders. Many city events.
- Network: roughly 5,000 YC founders, and he says you can DM any of them (for example the Airbnb founder, with a good reason) for help.
- Mindset: meeting founders who sold companies for $300M to $600M "unlocks your brain" about what is possible.
- Demo Day: GojiBerry raised money at a high valuation and diluted very little. Romàn says they now own about 85% of the company, do not plan to raise more, and have lots of cash to go all in once they find how to scale their channels.
- His view: raising at a high valuation while giving up little is a faster path to $10M or $20M than staying bootstrapped.
- Partner advice (his partner was Andrew Miklas, whose company IPO'd): talk to customers a lot, do not build features before talking to them, do not spend money if it is not profitable, do not hire too fast, fire fast if it is not working, and be all in. The partner also had a similar business in the same niche, so knew acquisition and how to talk to those users.
- Specific priorities come as hints, not orders, such as "maybe you should prioritize this because that company did that, but talk to your users."

chunks.heading: Mindset after $300k MRR
chunks.text:
- Romàn says he does not feel successful. The jump from $50k to $300k MRR changed little, and they are far from their objective.
- The team celebrated neither $1M nor $3M ARR despite promising to celebrate.
- He no longer plans to sell the company. He enjoys building and testing channels, and works in the office from 8 a.m. to 1 a.m.
- If they achieved a third of what they are doing now, he says he would still be very happy. He would not change anything about the path so far.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Roman explains why his first SaaS failed (no customer talks), how a cloned Shopify app reached $500K/yr and sold, and how he pre-sold a lead service before coding Goji Berry. Covers his cold outreach stack, blueprint offer, multi-channel distribution and a 90-day plan for new B2B founders.

chunks.heading: Validating before building: customer first, then sell before code
chunks.text:
- Romàn's core rule: "Everything starts with the customer, not with the product." A good idea comes from listening to the right people: how badly do they want the problem solved, and how much will they pay?
- His first SaaS failed. His team copied "One Text" (a YC-backed text-to-buy company), rebuilt it on WhatsApp for Europe, and spent 6 months building. Pilots stopped fast because European customers weren't ready to pay by text. He says one week of customer conversations would have shown that.
- He now treats having money before code as the signal: "having money before you code is a great sign. It means that really you are into something."
- Copying only works if the clone targets a real problem and the right audience. He warns against copying a company without knowing its unfair advantage, since its numbers may be misleading.
- Goji Berry went through V1 (AI UGC, reached about $500 MRR, no interest in evolving it) and V2 (a note taker like Fireflies, built as an MVP in about two weeks, very hard to sell) before V3. For V3 the developer waited while the two non-technical founders sold for the first month.

chunks.heading: Cloning a proven product and launching in two weeks
chunks.text:
- After the failed text-to-buy product, his team looked for WhatsApp tools already selling in Europe and making real money, rather than inventing a product.
- Finding them: one founder shared numbers on LinkedIn. The Chrome extension Store Leads shows which stores install a Shopify app, and team size also signals revenue. He searched "WhatsApp" in the Shopify App Store and created an account in each competing app.
- He picked the most successful app that was easiest to clone with what the team had already built. They implemented two main features in about two weeks.
- He re-contacted everyone from the text-to-buy outreach and landed 5 to 10 clients almost immediately, because almost no one sold it in France.
- The text-to-buy build had been harder than the competing apps, so adapting a few features and rules was enough. He describes the result as not the best product, but one that worked.

chunks.heading: Cold outreach engine: volume, targeting and the customer-service trick
chunks.text:
- Goji Berry's earlier product, Coco AI, got its early traction almost entirely from cold outreach, mostly in France. His daily list: about 100 calls, 1,000 to 2,000 cold emails, demos, and LinkedIn outreach.
- Demos closed at 60 to 70%, so the game was getting demos. Outside France, close rates fell to about 15 to 20% (Germany, Spain), which made scaling harder.
- ICP: Shopify stores making over $10K/month in Europe, with AI-tool users a plus.
- Lead sources: LinkedIn (people sharing results, then everyone interacting with them), Sales Navigator, Store Leads, Fox Leads.
- His scaling trick: email the customer service address with a demo video and ask them to forward it to the CEO. They almost always do, the CEO books a call, and replies come back nearly 100% of the time because support always answers, so emails avoid spam and volume can be high.
- Tools today: Goji AI (their own) with 5 LinkedIn accounts, plus Instantly for email, about 5,500 messages a day combined. At the start you don't need that much; one LinkedIn account and a few inboxes is enough.
- Why outreach ranks first: you know right away whether it works. If 5,000 emails get no answers, the offer or messaging is bad. Unlike Reddit or YouTube, it scales fast.
- Once a campaign has good response rates, he leaves the copy alone until it dies. His weekly job is adding leads and replying to people.

chunks.heading: The "blueprint" offer in cold messages
chunks.text:
- Instead of asking for a demo, which he finds intrusive for strangers, he writes the same email but offers a blueprint at the end.
- Saying yes to a blueprint is easier than saying yes to a demo, so most say yes.
- The blueprint is about 10 pages, full of value, with a booking link at the end.
- Most readers don't book a call; they go to the site and start a free trial. He says this puts the offer in front of more people than a demo ask.

chunks.heading: Selling before building: the $7K pre-code playbook
chunks.text:
- Trigger: Coco AI worked because outreach targeted high-intent leads, such as people commenting on LinkedIn posts about WhatsApp or email marketing. They were far more responsive.
- He emailed roughly 20,000 people across many industries in the US, offering high-intent leads, with a refund promise if it didn't work. He charged $200 to $300/month for 100 to 200 leads.
- After each call, buyers paid, and only then did he figure out delivery: manually first, then with a coworker, then Fiverr workers following an exact blueprint.
- Example blueprint: for a dental clinic hiring nurses, search "dental clinic nurse" on LinkedIn, collect people interacting, extract the right ones, find email and phone, send the lead list. Clients were happy because lead quality was high.
- He reached $7,000 before writing code. Demand grew until it was unmanageable, so they paused almost everything, then built the platform and automated it.
- Timeline: sold Coco AI in February, launched Goji Berry V3 in September. He says restarting is painful and that great products with low churn are hard to rebuild.

chunks.heading: Distribution: add channels one at a time, starting with Reddit
chunks.text:
- He disagrees with the "focus on one or two channels" advice, especially early. His process: post a lot on one channel, learn how it works, then keep adding channels while time per channel shrinks.
- Goji Berry grew from 0 to $33K MRR in 4 months and reached $50K in about 6, with channels added in this order: Reddit, outreach, X, SEO, YouTube, Trustmrr ads, and most recently Threads.
- Reddit: about 11 million impressions in 4 months, driving tens of thousands of visitors. It costs nothing but ChatGPT and storytelling. He posted 3 times a week across 10 SaaS subreddits.
- Formula: tell a story, back it with proof, include a link. Examples: a post on applying to Y Combinator and being rejected after the interview (what they did, what YC said, proof, link), and a post sharing a five-influencer campaign playbook with budget and results.
- Every business experiment (customer service, sales) becomes a Reddit post.
- Hack: get about 10 upvotes fast. A WhatsApp group of friends shares each new post so everyone upvotes it.
- Reddit, YouTube and similar channels are hard to scale (three posts a week won't become 30), which is why outreach stays number one.

chunks.heading: Paid and partner channels: influencers, newsletters, affiliates, Trustmrr
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn influencers beat newsletters. They have fewer deals, so prices can be cut in half or doubled in posts, and one or two customers can repay the spend. One viral post makes it very profitable, which a newsletter can't do. Finding them: keyword search and checking who sponsors competitors.
- Newsletters (French only so far): profitable over two to three months, payback in about three months, "not incredible". Attribution is hard. More competition from other SaaS.
- Affiliates: 30% lifetime commission, planning to raise to 40%, 50%, even 60%. Higher commissions attract more promoters and add visibility. New affiliates get a kit of videos to repost and text to paste, because most don't know how to promote. Affiliates are 10 to 15% of revenue, and he calls it under-worked. Recruiting is just a site link and occasional emails.
- Trustmrr ad: even if the ad didn't pay, posting about it on X would. Marc Lou retweeting the product twice brought many customers and leads. The ad itself brings a client every two to three days. A retweet from a founder with many followers beat the ad cost.

chunks.heading: 90-day plan if starting B2B SaaS from scratch
chunks.text:
- Start from your skills and unfair advantage. Study how competitors market and whether they raised funds or bootstrapped, then pick your own path.
- Build 7 PowerPoint slides: logo, pain points, solution, how the product works, price.
- Message 100 to 500 people, get them on calls, and ask about their problems. Pain points usually differ from the slide. Adapt each time.
- When someone will pay, deliver it as a service, or promise to build it and then find a co-founder or paid developer. Validate with 5 to 10 people before going all in.
- Marketing: first cold outreach, with a LinkedIn automation tool and email tool at about $300 to $500 total, aiming for 10 more demos. When it can run near autopilot, add inbound on LinkedIn, X and Reddit (e.g. a Reddit post on how you're solving the problem, asking for feedback).
- Month 1: outreach. Month 2: outreach plus inbound. Month 3: more traffic sources, maybe paid or influencers, depending on money. He notes this is harder with zero capital.
- What moves the needle: do more of what works. If 10 messages yield one demo, send 100, then 1,000. He says people underestimate the energy needed.

chunks.heading: Selling a SaaS and building a team
chunks.text:
- Coco AI reached $500K/year and sold for seven figures about two years after starting. Reasons: only France was reachable, other markets closed at 15 to 20%, two teammates wanted to sell, and he had no long-term vision for the product.
- Marketplaces like Acquire.com and Flippa gave offers of a quarter or third of the final price because it lacked a year of revenue. He instead contacted Shopify app founders with portfolios of apps, then answered a LinkedIn post from a buyer looking for businesses in his size range. The sale closed about two months later: 90% upfront, 10% over three years.
- He credits both work and luck.
- Team: four at Coco AI (two marketing, one product, one code), three at Goji Berry (one each). The code is not his part and he doesn't discuss tech tools.
- Goji Berry now has about 500 customers. The plan is a GTM copilot that tells you whom, when and how to contact, rather than only sending messages, with a lean team and no hiring soon.
- He knows what he wants to build because he's done outreach for five years and is the product's core user.
- Mistakes: building something customers didn't want (Coco AI), moving too fast on marketing and paying fake influencers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn Czerny recounts selling his WhatsApp e-commerce SaaS Cocoai (about $50k MRR, sold for over $1M) and killing two failed ideas before finding Gojiberry, a buying-signal tool. He explains how he validates by pre-selling, why he copies proven products, and where he sees SaaS opportunities in sales tooling and US micro-niches.

chunks.heading: Why Romàn chose SaaS over infopreneurship and Web3
chunks.text:
- He is 30 and has done freelancing, infoproducts, and a Web3 venture (a raised round for a mobile game) before settling on SaaS about 2.5 years ago.
- His reasoning: past 25, you cannot relaunch a project or switch sector every 3 years, so you need something durable.
- SaaS gives revenue that is "quasiment très prédictible" (monthly or annual payers).
- It decouples the business from personal branding: customers buy the product, not him. He is replaceable, so the company is sellable.
- He says the leverage of 3 years in SaaS is far bigger than 3 years in infopreneurship.
- On Web3: friends made fortunes, but many projects failed and he took out almost nothing. He calls it "pile ou face", hard to make durable, and dependent on raising a lot of money at the right moment.
- SaaS can be built over 5 to 10 years (some for 20, like Salesforce) with large valuations.
- He likes earning online without showing his face much.

chunks.heading: Cocoai: copy a validated product, pivot fast, sell at about €1M+
chunks.text:
- First attempt: he picked a Y Combinator startup from 2023 (One Text, "text to buy" via SMS) and adapted it. It failed in Europe: customers answered "yes" and did not understand why they were billed. About 6 months were lost.
- His lesson: YC backs about 500 companies a year and can afford 450 failures, so copying one YC startup is roulette. Also, you cannot transpose a US product directly.
- Pivot: he copied competitors already winning in Europe on WhatsApp and built "the same thing, better". First customers came right after the pivot, with very little churn.
- Outcome: about $50k MRR after roughly 8 months from first customers, sold for "plus d'un million".
- Why he sold:
  - Platform risk: WhatsApp depends on Meta, which changes rules and prices about every 3 months. Marketing messages were banned in the US during the sale process.
  - Part of the team was losing interest.
- Founder-side caveat: he sees the pivot from his own instinct to "copy what works" as a reaction to Web3 trauma ("j'ai trop fait confiance à mon instinct").

chunks.heading: How he sold the company
chunks.text:
- He ran a Boolean search on LinkedIn for people with "buying SaaS" in their bio and contacted them. The first to answer became the buyer.
- The buyer had been looking for a Shopify SaaS for months and partnered with a fund.
- Timeline: a call, then about 2 months of due diligence with lawyers and many emails, described as smooth.
- Terms: 90% upfront, 10% paid over 3 years from the company's profits (he calls it not a true earn-out).
- The buyer paid lawyers (about $15k) and registration costs.
- Proceeds went up into holdings, reinvested within the legal window (he recalls about 70%, and says to check the exact figure), so no immediate tax. He sees it as "des points de vie" to build other projects for 10 years.
- Post-sale lesson: the US buyer communicated in English with a base that was about 60% French. Revenue fell about 15% below the sale level before recovering. Cultural and language fit matters when selling abroad.

chunks.heading: Killing two SaaS fast before Gojiberry
chunks.text:
- Gojiberry V1 (AI UGC videos): LinkedIn posts got several million views and 3,000 to 4,000 signups but only 4 or 5 paying customers, about €300 MRR.
  - He killed it within a week. It attracted the curious, solved no deep need, and he saw no brand using it long term.
  - Generation costs were high, so margins were weak.
- V2 (AI call recorder, like Fireflies and tl;dv): built in 2 weeks, sold roughly $300 to $400 MRR.
  - Every demo asked "what's different?" and he had no answer. He used Fireflies himself.
  - Those companies burn their funding on transcription, and selling $20 licences to non-decision-makers is painful.
  - He killed it as well.
- Principle: he was looking for an explosive project, not a slow grind.

chunks.heading: Gojiberry V3: sell before you build
chunks.text:
- Choosing the need: the most pressing need across all his conversations was "more customers". "N'importe quel business te dira: si je peux avoir plus de clients, je suis chaud."
- Product idea: detect buying signals (for example people interacting with certain LinkedIn posts), then enrich the contact with email and phone. He copied a US YC-backed, profitable company, Origami. Many signal tools do not enrich contacts, and that is the gap he filled.
- Validation: he got on a call with Origami as a mystery client. The rep spent 30 minutes explaining why he would not sell, which signalled strong demand.
- Pre-sale: a Lovable landing page that simulated the output (his own prompts, no software). Emailed to prospects, it brought $3,000 to $4,000 in the first week, at about $500 per customer, before a line of code was written.
- Inspiration: a free course by Adam Robinson (Retention.com, Warmly-style visitor identification), who offered the idea at a conference and people handed over their cards.
- Rule: "je coderais pas une seule ligne avant qu'on me donne de l'argent", even with AI.
- Targets: B2B teams at companies with 100M+ revenue.
- Growth: about 25% per week, about 250 clients, one French. US only.
- Unfair advantage: his developer had already built LinkedIn signal extraction and multi-account management, worth 6 to 12 months of head start.
- Why V3 beat V1 and V2: sales is a need felt immediately, whereas accounting or HR tools come later.

chunks.heading: Gojiberry growth and sales stack
chunks.text:
- Team: 3 full time plus 2 freelancers about to become employees.
- Early manual phase: for 2 weeks he used 5 Pakistani freelancers on Fiver, following a protocol, to find buying signals before the product existed.
- Channel mix: cold email and outreach drive about 60 to 70% of demos, and the other 30 to 40% is inbound (Reddit, LinkedIn).
- Stack:
  - Gojiberry to scrape leads who like or comment on topics like cold mailing and lead generation, and to enrich them.
  - Instantly for cold email: 3,000 to 4,000 emails a day, scaling up. AI pre-replies overnight; he reviews and sends about 500 in 2 minutes.
  - Walaxy for LinkedIn outreach campaigns on the same leads.
  - WhatsApp messages (or calls for French prospects) to hot leads.
  - Reddit posting, automated, which brings a lot of demos.
- Dogfooding: using the product to grow the company is "la meilleure preuve au monde".
- Leverage: AI lets him do the work of about five marketers from a few years ago.

chunks.heading: Copilot AI, not full AI, and why SaaS survives LLMs
chunks.text:
- Copilot vs full AI: he does not believe in 100% AI sales agents ("AI SDR"). AI is better than humans at lead generation, but personalisation needs judgment.
  - Example: if one contact does not reply, a human adds their manager, takes both phone numbers, checks their comments, and phones.
  - He advises calling people with a human voice.
- Argument that SaaS is not dead:
  - ChatGPT launched a note taker and everyone said it would kill note-taking tools, yet a month later Fireflies and tl;dv were still growing.
  - Mainstream features evangelise the category, and niche buyers then look for specialised tools.
  - People who say "I can do it with n8n" ignore maintenance. A 2,000-person company would not pay someone $5k to $7k a month to maintain it, versus his $500 tool.
  - A friend's SaaS launched 10 years ago was told "WordPress does it free" and now makes tens of millions a year. DIY people do not pay.
  - He reasons that VCs invest millions in SaaS with multi-year visibility.
  - Customers still value UX, an experience, continuity, and a human to talk to.
- Warning: incumbents without AI (a friend's large SaaS) face new entrants that replicate in 1.5 years what took 10.
- Vibe-coding tools: he sees Lovable as good for demos and videos, not a replacement for a developer. He has not replaced his own.
- Founder advice: SaaS is "niveau 2". Take a technical cofounder; a paid dev will never be as committed as someone with skin in the game.
- Capital: you need runway because you won't pay yourself. He says at least €30k to €50k, since tools alone (Instantly about $500 a month, an accountant, AI licences) add up.

chunks.heading: SaaS ideas and niches he sees
chunks.text:
- Pre-warmed mailboxes for cold email: a huge demand, and few suppliers (mostly India, Pakistan, some US). "Chaque personne à qui je parle de cold email me pose cette question". Instantly likely marks up its own heavily.
- Reddit keyword monitoring with AI-drafted comments (he uses Popsy, YC-backed, with competitors): a similar signals idea applied to Reddit.
- Cheaper LinkedIn outreach copilot: existing tools (Waalaxy-like) are expensive and make you write the messages. He sees room for a cheaper tool with AI credits and pre-written messages.
- Vertical SaaS in the US: depth of market lets micro-niches reach multi-million exits. Examples: a SaaS for landscapers only in Florida sold for about $20M to $30M; a vet note-taking tool valued at hundreds of millions; therapist booking software making about €120k MRR (told secondhand).
  - A niche lets you target a message, build a network, and ship features generalist tools skip. A US state is as deep as France.
- AI email assistant by niche: Fixer-style tools pre-answer a Gmail inbox. He suggests niching it for construction trades.
- Consumer apps: Cal AI (calorie scanning, a ChatGPT wrapper) is marketing-driven, using around $50/year plans. He advises against cloning it: the barrier is low (about €2,000 to rebuild) but copying marketing genius is not possible.
- Distribution check before choosing a niche: he dropped a restaurant answering-machine idea because restaurateurs are very hard to reach. Ask how you will reach the target first (for example Facebook groups for vets).
- Source of ideas: YC's twice-yearly manifestos on trends, since they now back companies already making money. He says AI agents are the main theme, in copilot or full-AI versions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Roman, co-founder and CMO of Gojiberry, explains how he validated the product by manually finding leads for paying customers before building. He covers outreach on intent signals instead of static databases, a Reddit-to-multichannel funnel, lead magnet and webinar distribution, and paywalling AI SaaS to control costs.

chunks.heading: Validate with real revenue before building: manual fulfillment, payment links, then outbound
chunks.text:
- Romàn's rule: "Don't build anything unless people want to pay you." If people are not throwing their credit cards at you, you don't have the right product.
- Gojiberry's third version (V3) was sold before it was built. V1 (UGC) lasted two weeks; V2 (a note-taker, chasing the Fireflies trend) lasted one month and was "really hard to sell".
- For V3 the developer told the founders to sell the solution first and he would build it once customers existed.
- Romàn pitched companies on high-intent leads and delivered manually: he searched LinkedIn lead by lead, about 24 hours of work per 100 leads, at $100/month per customer.
- That manual service reached $10k MRR in about two months. Then they told every customer the service was shutting down and relaunched it as a platform, which is when growth took off.
- Revenue also motivated the developer, since it proved people wanted to buy.
- He says too many people "build something no one wants and they hide behind the fact that they are building".
- Early customers say "I'd love to use it when it's out" to be nice. The real test is to send a payment link to secure their spot. If most pay, it is validated; some will not.
- Goal for new founders in 2026: get traffic to a landing page as fast as possible and validate; don't procrastinate.

chunks.heading: Early go-to-market sequence: outbound first, then funnel, then volume
chunks.text:
- Phase 1, validation: for the first 10-50 customers he does everything outbound (calls, emails, LinkedIn requests) and doesn't communicate on social media at all.
- He takes demos even for $50-$100 customers, to learn who they are, why they said yes and what they want.
- He "would never start a SaaS without doing calls at the beginning, even if it's painful".
- Phase 2, funnel: once he knows what people want, he builds a funnel for that audience and pushes volume in to see where it breaks and where people drop off. He tests several prices.
- Phase 3, scale: with a working funnel, "you only need more people". If 1,000 visitors produce X revenue, the game becomes impressions and signups.
- He is cash-conscious: Gojiberry is profitable and had not spent any YC money by the time of the interview, so he doesn't spend money he doesn't have to make things go faster.

chunks.heading: Reddit as a volume and validation channel
chunks.text:
- Romàn created roughly 2,000 posts on Reddit, pushing hard.
- It brought about 2,000 visitors per day. Reddit traffic is "not so qualitative", but the volume was enough to find who converts and how they behave in the funnel.
- Posts were advice-style content on outreach, sales and marketing, run from many accounts.
- He estimates Reddit alone took them from zero to $20K MRR.
- Limit: showing up 10 times a day everywhere hurts the brand, so they expanded to X, LinkedIn and cold email once Reddit had validated the funnel and told them who pays.

chunks.heading: Current Gojiberry acquisition channels
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn lead-magnet posts: the team posts many of them, and they bring many customers. LinkedIn traffic is far more qualified than X or Reddit for an outreach SaaS.
- The lead-magnet recipe: post a result ("I helped a website rank top 10 on Google in under six months"), tell people to comment a keyword (e.g. "SEO") for the recipe, reply to each commenter with a Notion link containing a video of who you are, what you solve and a book-a-demo CTA. More engagement means more Notion visits, website visits and customers.
- X: two founders have large followings and go viral about weekly. It works for founders, solo founders and SMBs of 1-10 (maybe 20) people, with higher churn but an effectively infinite lead pool. It doesn't reach heads of sales, who don't self-identify on X.
- Other channels: YouTube, a webinar three times a week, B2B influencers on LinkedIn, a bit of Meta ads, the YC exposure, word of mouth.
- Affiliates bring about a quarter to a fifth of revenue.
- Paid placement: they paid a well-known X creator for mentions and a TrustMRR listing. About $1,500 spent produced around $1,000 of new MRR per month, profitable but small at their stage; they keep it for staying top of mind.

chunks.heading: Webinars instead of one-on-one demos
chunks.text:
- Every marketing asset (blueprints, SEO pages, influencer docs) links to the webinar, which runs three times a week with about 40 people per session.
- They stopped one-on-one calls because they didn't scale for customers paying $100-$200 per month.
- Format: explain high-intent leads and the results possible, demo the product for 15 minutes, answer chat questions, and invite a customer on stage to present their business.
- Romàn says he likes marketing but not sales, and finds webinars energizing because he runs the show.

chunks.heading: YouTube: rank for competitor "review" searches
chunks.text:
- Strategy: publish videos titled "[competitor name] review 2026" and spend about 10 minutes reviewing their SaaS.
- Mid-video he says "we have an alternative" (Gojiberry), and viewers sign up. He compares it to Google ads, but free.
- Output: about 60 videos since January against a goal of one per day; he admits he is behind.

chunks.heading: Cold email and outreach tactics
chunks.text:
- High-intent leads: Gojiberry finds leads who engaged with a competitor, a keyword or specific influencers. He says once you've tried high-intent leads you "can never go back to a cold database".
- Reply rates run two to five times those of competitors using static databases. Targeting active leads alone gives about 2x; adding personalized messages and an aligned LinkedIn profile (good picture, clear line) gives 4-5x.
- Scraping 1,000 people from Apollo or Sales Navigator yields maybe 100 who might be interested. Some are inactive on LinkedIn, changed jobs or don't care.
- Volume: about 6,000 emails per day for Gojiberry's own outreach. It is capped by how many people show intent each day. Gojiberry itself is used for low-volume warm outreach (roughly 20 personalized messages per day), and he uses Instantly for cold email.
- Best current campaign: pay B2B influencers to post lead-magnet posts on LinkedIn, then retarget every liker and commenter by cold email: "I saw you commented on this post. Maybe you didn't get the resource, would you like me to send it again?" It gets an "insane" reply rate and keeps them top of mind.
- Earlier variant: pull the commenters of competitors' lead-magnet posts (some had 3,000 commenters), email "did you get the blueprint?", then mention his own blueprint on the same subject; people usually say send yours.
- Copy rules: messages are short, about three lines. The lead should not need to think more than two seconds. Use a low-friction CTA like "I've done X for Y, I can show you how. Reply yes and I'll send it to you", not "How are you addressing sales at your company?"
- Subject lines: don't trick people ("your order is here", "your Meta ad has been banned"), which is a red flag for bigger companies. Examples he uses: "you commented, here is your blueprint", "did you get it". He admits he should A/B test headlines more.
- AI vs human copy: about 80% of users get better results from AI-written messages because they don't know what to write. In his own five campaigns, AI sometimes beats his hand-written ones, so he runs a mix.
