chunks.heading: Free trials, paywalls and AI-SaaS pricing
chunks.text:
- AI SaaS has real token costs, so free usage attracts users (he cites India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, sometimes South America) who use it heavily but can't pay.
- Gojiberry's setup: a paywall at signup, credit card required, 7-day free trial. If seven days isn't enough, support in chat gives 14.
- Even so, India is their third-largest nationality of signups, and only 2-3% of those pay, versus an average of 40% overall.
- His point: with free AI usage, people will use it free and you can't blame them.

chunks.heading: Selling a SaaS: lessons from the Koko AI exit
chunks.text:
- Koko AI did WhatsApp marketing and AI chat for e-commerce brands and went from zero to $500K in a few months. Churn was low, but nearly all customers were French. A competitor held the upmarket, leaving them mid and low market, and two of the co-founders wanted out.
- The buyer was found when Romàn reached out on LinkedIn to people with "looking to buy a SaaS" in their bio; contacts passed the word along. The sale to an American buyer took two months. The buyer doubled the business by finding US customers.
- Lesson: when a buyer really wants you, they move fast.
- Due diligence prep: have accounting in order, because a mess slows it down. Keep personal expenses out of the company, since buyers go through every bank-statement line to check your story.
- Keep the buyer's attention during the process: send updates (e.g. "just closed a customer"), because buyers usually run several due diligences at once and you need to stay the best option.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Román Czerny, co-founder of Goji Berry AI, explains how his team finds high-intent LinkedIn leads and turns them into meetings. He covers active-lead targeting, giving value before asking for a demo, lead-magnet distribution across channels, and funnel numbers (about 70% demo close, 35% trial to paid).

chunks.heading: Who Romàn is and how Goji Berry AI came about
chunks.text:
- Romàn Czerny is 30, a mechanical engineer who worked at a car manufacturer before going into entrepreneurship in 2019. He is from Normandy, France, and lives in Lisbon, Portugal.
- Path: freelance, then affiliate marketing, then SaaS in 2022. His first SaaS, Koko AI, was sold to a US venture.
- While building Koko AI, his team found a way to book more demos by targeting the right people. That became Goji Berry AI (Goji).
- He is a co-founder and the marketer on the team. His day runs from about 9:00 a.m. to 10 p.m.

chunks.heading: Positioning: finding high-intent leads and contacting them in one tool
chunks.text:
- Goji finds high-intent leads and helps contact them on LinkedIn.
- Outreach tools such as Heyreach and Lemlist only automate the sending. Intent tools such as ZoomInfo and Warmly find the leads but are expensive and built for enterprise.
- Romàn saw no affordable tool for small businesses that did both. That is the gap Goji fills.
- Goji adds AI at every step, instead of "put the leads here and we'll outreach them".

chunks.heading: How the Goji workflow works
chunks.text:
1. An AI agent is configured with an ideal customer profile (ICP), either written by hand or generated with AI.
2. The user picks intent signals to track:
   - interactions with the company's LinkedIn page or profile
   - profile visits and new page followers
   - keywords and topics a person is talking about or engaging with
   - interactions with competitor companies or their posts
   - people who just changed jobs
   - people at companies that just raised funds
3. Each day Goji delivers new leads to a dashboard. Every lead carries its signal and an AI score. For example, someone who just followed the Goji page and fits the ICP scores high.
4. The leads shown are heavily filtered. Romàn says six leads shown might come from about 600 people who interacted with posts.
5. AI writes a personalized message per lead from the signal, company and background.
6. The campaign is sent. Leads are ranked so the warmest are contacted first. A unified inbox shows who is interested.

- Romàn notes most outreach targets job title plus location only. Adding what the lead is talking about or interacting with is the difference.
- The team keeps swapping in the latest AI model: ChatGPT, then Gemini, now Claude.

chunks.heading: Why Claude Code alone does not replace a tool like this
chunks.text:
- If you ask Claude to scroll LinkedIn posts and collect leads yourself, LinkedIn will block you. Claude is "not a tool made to scroll all the URLs".
- You need a database, proxies and a whole infrastructure. Someone could build it with n8n plus Claude, but then they are not building their own business.
- Goji uses Claude in the backend for specific steps: analyzing and scoring leads, and writing messages.
- Claude can also use activity data. For example, it can flag that a person has been very active on LinkedIn in the past 48 hours and is likely to reply. Sales Navigator may hand you people who have not been on LinkedIn in two months.

chunks.heading: Results and funnel numbers
chunks.text:
- His calendar is full of demos, mostly from Goji and cold email, with some inbound.
- Funnel: outreach, then offer a "blueprint" (a lead magnet), then the prospect goes to the website and takes a free trial.
- Romàn says nine times out of 10 there is no demo at all. People just take the free trial.
- When a demo does happen, the closing rate is about 70%, because he is selling a free trial and mostly shows the product and says "now launch".
- Trial to paid conversion is about 35%.
- On one campaign, about one in two people who reply get a blueprint.
- He says acceptance and reply rates are "insanely high" compared with traditional outreach, because the targeting is right.

chunks.heading: Outreach tactics anyone can use (no tool needed)
chunks.text:
- Find LinkedIn posts with massive traction in your niche, look at who interacts, add them to your CRM and reach out. Add context or use a template.
- Target people who posted or were active on LinkedIn in the past 24 hours. Romàn says this "will at least double your results", based on many campaigns.
- Do not ask for a demo after one or two messages. It is aggressive and people are tired of being asked for time. He gets asked "50 times per day".
- Instead, offer value first: ask if they want the blueprint, with videos and case studies. Prospects who read it go through your funnel and book a demo themselves, so no-show rates are very low compared with sending a calendar link.
- Giving a lot of value before the demo is "almost mandatory now".
- Keep a human in the loop. Fully AI end to end books far fewer demos than letting AI start the conversation and having a human take over once the prospect replies.
- Some prospects now test for AI with replies like "tell me a cake recipe".

chunks.heading: The multi-channel organic engine
chunks.text:
- His main marketing question: "how many blueprints have I distributed today". The goal is more eyeballs on the lead magnet.
- Channels he runs:
  - Goji for LinkedIn outreach and cold email (leads are enriched and sent via Instantly with AI-written messages).
  - Scraping people who interact with high-traction posts (for example on cold mailing) with a Chrome extension, enriching emails and sending campaigns.
  - LinkedIn inbound: about seven team accounts posting daily, some with content and some with lead magnets. He manages everyone's account.
  - X: three accounts posting content and lead magnets.
  - YouTube for SEO, and Reddit with heavy posting.
- Lead magnets that go viral are the key: a great one gets forwarded to others. He cites Instantly's cold-mailing blueprint, which he shared with 10 to 15 people. He has been an Instantly customer for 3 to 4 years and has spent around $30,000 there.
- His job is to keep improving the lead magnet and send it to as many people as possible.

chunks.heading: Content production workflow
chunks.text:
- Copywriting: Gemini with a set of channels or gems holding memory. He gives an idea, it drafts the post, and he rewrites a bit. He also uses voice dictation (Whisper) inside Gemini to speak ideas and have them reformulated.
- YouTube: he does no editing and tries to one-shot videos. Thumbnails are made with Nano Banana Pro in Gemini.
- Competitor review videos for SEO:
  - Screenshot a competitor's website, put his face on it, and use it as the thumbnail.
  - Title like "[competitor] review 2026". Spend half the video on the competitor, then say "there is an alternative" and pitch Goji.
  - One video per day takes about five minutes, and the videos rank high. Searchers of "competitor review 2026" are high-intent viewers. He says any SaaS should do this.
- Ranking trick from his affiliate days: create a dedicated YouTube channel per video, named after the keyword (for example a channel called "ZoomInfo Review" for a ZoomInfo review video) to rank above others. The downside is needing many channels.

chunks.heading: Views on AI agents
chunks.text:
- Open-source agents like OpenClaw are still known mostly in tech circles. An average owner of a 20-person company in France knows ChatGPT and not much more.
- He admits that in about five years software might do what Goji does from one prompt. Things move fast, which he finds exciting and scary.
- If prospects' inboxes become AI too, booking demos gets harder, which is why he keeps a human taking over replies for now.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Roman explains why LinkedIn outreach should target only high-intent leads (right ICP, recently active, showing a signal) instead of sending more volume. He walks through signal and lookalike agents, how to prune weak keywords, and the low-friction "can I send you a blueprint?" message that drives his best demo flow.

chunks.heading: Roman's LinkedIn intent-signal outreach model (Goji Berry)
chunks.text:
- Roman is co-founder of Goji Berry (Goji AI), started with three people in August. Roman reports about 1,800 customers, mainly in the US, plus France and Europe.
- Before Goji, he sold a SaaS called Koko AI (WhatsApp for e-commerce, aimed at Shopify merchants). No database or Sales Navigator list was good enough, so he hand-picked leads on LinkedIn.
- His manual method: type keywords like "Klaviyo" or "fulfillment e-commerce", see who interacts with them, and build a lead list one by one. He later realized this was already high-intent outreach.
- His definition of a signal: the right job title and location, active on LinkedIn in the past 48 hours, plus some intent.
- He ranks intent from low to high:
  - Active on LinkedIn in the past 48 hours (already roughly doubles response).
  - Interacted with a competitor or a specific keyword.
  - Just hired, just fundraised, or interacting with an industry leader.
  - Viewed your profile or followed your company page (warmest).
- Goji works the warmest signals first.
- His thesis: reply and connection rates on traditional outreach keep falling. There are two ways to book more demos:
  - Volume: cold email, for example 10,000 emails a day (he does this too), at the risk of burning accounts.
  - Targeting: on LinkedIn you can only reach about 200 connections a week, so maximize the return on those 200 by contacting only high-intent leads.

chunks.heading: Setting up signal agents
chunks.text:
- Goji's flow has four steps: set up an agent, get contacts, send the campaign, handle replies in the inbox.
- A signal agent starts with ICP filters (for example developers in San Francisco in SaaS), then adds tracked signals.
- Signals he lists:
  - Engagement with your own page or profile.
  - Profile views and new company-page followers.
  - Keywords or topics (people who like, comment on or post about them).
  - Specific LinkedIn profiles, such as an industry expert whose audience cares about LinkedIn outreach but may not know Goji exists.
  - Competitor pages (he tracks HubSpot-style pages).
  - Companies that raised funds and people who changed jobs.
  - A "top active profiles in your ICP" option.
- Keyword signals track what people engage with, not what they say themselves. Likes mean they liked posts with the keyword, comments mean they commented, and posts mean they posted.
- GDPR example: a data officer engaging with GDPR posts is a reason to reach out about what they may be doing wrong.
- The "most active profiles" signal samples about 2,000 ICP members and returns only the top fraction (shown as 5%, in practice closer to 0.1%). It suits niches with no keyword signals, such as HR people in Norway. It is lower intent, but those people will see the connection request.
- A signal agent can track at most 15 signals.
- Volume target: at least 25 leads per day, enough to feed 25 daily outreach actions.
- Optimization loop:
  - Once demos arrive, check which keyword or signal produced them.
  - Delete keywords that produce zero leads and replace them.
  - Review the launch history (leads scanned vs. leads that made the cut) and the per-signal insights.
- Sample numbers from his own account: 239 leads scanned and 5 kept; 305 scanned and 8 kept; some keywords returned zero out of 264 or 61 and were candidates for removal. A zero from a person or page can mean it is inactive (for example, a banned company page).
- If an agent returns no leads, he suggests switching from "high precision" to "discovery". Discovery gives broader matches, including adjacent roles.
- He hasn't touched his own agents in about six months because results were fine; low-volume keywords need changing more often.

chunks.heading: Lookalike agents and segmenting by awareness
chunks.text:
- A lookalike agent starts from the LinkedIn URL of your best customer. It matches on industry, country, job title and behavior on LinkedIn, and can include similar roles or related industries.
- It runs daily and finds more leads with a match percentage. It gives less control than signal agents, but it's useful for finding ICP matches without tracking explicit signals.
- He separates agents by awareness so each gets its own campaign and results can be compared:
  - "Solution aware": people interacting with competitors.
  - "Super hot": people who interacted with his profile or page, viewed his profile or followed the company page, plus people interacting with his own team.
- His campaign results:
  - Solution-aware: 62% acceptance, 49% reply.
  - Super hot: 61% acceptance, 30% reply.
- For comparison, he says a great campaign on other tools is about 20% acceptance and 20% reply.
- Beyond signals, Goji also has an AI "ask" feature that searches the web (including Google News) for leads with a custom signal. His example: CEOs who run webinars, or companies that closed a Series B or above in San Francisco in the past month. The signal then becomes the personalization hook ("I saw you run weekly webinars").
- Leads can also be imported by CSV, via the Chrome extension from Sales Navigator, or from first-degree connections.
- He used first-degree connections early on, to get fast responses when starting a new business. He is cautious with them, and Goji limits messages to existing connections to 30 per day.

chunks.heading: Messaging: the blueprint / lead magnet play
chunks.text:
- His best-performing campaign asks permission to send a lead magnet instead of pitching. Example message: "Hello, I've just created a blueprint about how we get 12 demos per week using AI. Just reply yes and I'll send it to you." A variant: "we booked 12 demos in 5 days using warm leads plus on LinkedIn. I wrote a short doc breaking down exactly how we did it... Want me to send it over?"
- When someone replies yes, he sends a blueprint with a video of his face explaining what they do and how the lead can get value. At the bottom are a free-trial link and a demo-booking link.
- His view: "to get demos, the blueprint strategy is by far the best strategy in B2B SaaS."
- Why it works:
  - The reader should have to think as little as possible. A long message forces a 2-5 minute reply, which busy people won't give.
  - Replying "yes" costs almost nothing, while missing out on "how to get 12 demos a week" feels costly.
  - Even a little value in the resource keeps the lead engaged, so they watch videos and click links, and some convert.
- Goji's AI ice breaker names the intent signal that triggered, adds context, then asks for a conversation. Roman says it beats what about 90% of people write, so unless you're in the top 10% of outreach writers, it will beat your own first message. He prefers to follow up manually.
- One account of his sends only AI ice-breaker messages and reaches an acceptance rate that's high, with a 50% reply rate on AI messages.
- Other formats that he says perform well:
  - A CFO-focused breakfast invitation in a big European city (in person, closing many deals).
  - Personalized case studies.
  - Personalized Loom videos ("I made a video about your business, may I send it to you?").
- Campaign options in Goji include invitation notes, AI personalized messages, follow-ups, voice messages, profile visits and email (a multichannel addition). It doesn't support InMail yet. Campaigns can be generated by AI from a selected lead list, a goal (start conversations or book demos) and a tone.

chunks.heading: Account safety and profile quality
chunks.text:
- None of his roughly 1,800 customers has had a hard ban, he says. The risk comes from running multiple automation tools on one account or using a fake LinkedIn account that hasn't been warmed up (which may get locked and asked for an ID).
- He has used automation tools for about 10 years. The worst result was a LinkedIn message saying automation isn't allowed, about three years ago.
- His safety rules:
  - Use a residential proxy in your own country (Goji runs in the cloud from that country) so you aren't disconnected.
  - Respect recommended weekly limits, which vary by account type: new, active or Sales Navigator.
  - Messages are spread over about five hours instead of being sent in bursts.
- His reasoning: LinkedIn has no interest in banning people doing real business. High reply and connection rates are a good signal for the platform; only spam or nonsense gets restricted.
- Profile quality drives acceptance rate. Accounts with no picture, banner or job history see poor acceptance. A LinkedIn profile gives proof of identity that cold email lacks, and acts like a sales page for anyone who looks at it.

chunks.heading: Who the approach works for, and closing advice
chunks.text:
- Roman's customer mix: about 50% B2B SaaS (easy to find customers on LinkedIn), a large share of services and agencies, and about 25% brick-and-mortar businesses and professionals such as doctors and dentists.
- For brick-and-mortar, he says Goji works no worse than any other tool, but high-intent leads are scarce because plumbers and dentists aren't active on LinkedIn. He advises scraping Google Maps or using another tool for them.
- Closing advice: whether or not you use Goji, high-intent outreach beats volume. Take time to find leads, find a real reason to contact each, and personalize genuinely, because inboxes are flooded with AI nonsense. He says, "people are still looking to buy from humans."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A full walkthrough of GojiBerry's go-to-market: validate with a few slides and calls, start with outbound, then layer inbound, paid, SEO and demos. The common thread is lead magnets and high-intent targeting across LinkedIn, cold email, X, Reddit, YouTube and influencers.

chunks.heading: Validate before building
chunks.text:
- Romàn insists on validating the idea before writing code. He makes a 3-6 slide PowerPoint and takes calls with his ICP.
- The first signal is a prospect asking "how much is that?" at the end of the pitch. Willingness to pay is the real test.
- GojiBerry's version: he sold lead lists, manually finding high-intent leads for paying customers. When manual delivery got too hard, he built the product and added outreach.
- Channel order he recommends: start with outbound if you have no clients (fast feedback). Add inbound next, then paid once money comes in, and do SEO/GEO a bit every week to compound.
- GojiBerry reached $1M ARR in under 9 months with a multi-channel engine: inbound (LinkedIn, X, Reddit), outbound (LinkedIn, cold email), paid (Facebook/Meta ads, Trustmrr ads, influencers) and SEO/GEO (one freelancer plus one software).

chunks.heading: LinkedIn outreach with high-intent leads
chunks.text:
- First check that your customers are actually on LinkedIn.
- Limit: about 150-180 invitations per week per account, so targeting must be precise.
- ICP-only targeting (job title + country, e.g. "CFOs in the US") no longer works. Many profiles are inactive for 3+ months or outdated.
- High-intent targeting gets "three five times more responses". Intent signals: engaging with your profile or company, engaging with competitors, posting meaningful content, hiring, recent job changes, engaging with relevant keywords or specific profiles.
- Most outreach tools only send; he avoids static databases because "data moves very fast" and prefers dynamic, signal-based lead feeds (his own tool, GojiBerry).
- Accounts: any LinkedIn account works, ideally branded with a headline and active. Stay under limits, don't spam, use a residential proxy. Nobody on his team or among customers has been banned.
- Setup in GojiBerry: paste the website, connect a LinkedIn account, let the agent define the ICP, pick signals, set the objective (book qualified demos).
- Results shown: one campaign at 71% acceptance and 52% reply rate. He runs 8+ accounts, e.g. one sending 29 invitations and 30 messages per day.
- Expected funnel per account: 200 invitations/week gives ~50% acceptance (100 people), ~50% reply (50 people), then roughly 8-12 booked demos. Varies by offer and market.

chunks.heading: Cold email at 6,000 emails per day
chunks.text:
- Lead sources: (1) high-intent leads from GojiBerry, ~100-200 per day, enriched for emails; (2) scraping with the GojiBerry Chrome extension (Sales Navigator, post engagers, event attendees, search) then enrichment; (3) static databases like Apollo, which are easiest but get the fewest replies.
- Infrastructure: Instantly (used since 2022). About 124 inboxes across ~40 domains, 3 inboxes per domain, 50 emails per inbox per day (150 per domain). Buys pre-warmed or done-for-you accounts, never connects existing ones. Done-for-you domains look like the brand (e.g. a "team" version of the company domain) but need ~2 weeks warm-up.
- He doesn't optimize for cheap inboxes: "I'm trying to get business", so he pays for reliable infrastructure. Cost is about $500/month; one customer has lifetime value of roughly $400, so he needs one customer per month to break even.
- Results: 400,000+ emails sent, 1.43% reply rate excluding auto-replies.
- Content strategy: find what's hyped in the market, especially lead magnets that get thousands of LinkedIn comments, rebuild a similar blueprint, and email the same audience offering it (e.g. "I've built a blueprint about [topic]. Want to see it?"). Sequence is just 3 emails with varied wording and a simple signature.
- Settings: text-only emails, tracking of opens disabled (triggers spam filters), stop on auto-reply, prioritize new leads, send every day including Sunday (little competition, good replies).
- When someone replies, they get the blueprint plus demo video, screenshots, social proof and a booking link.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn inbound: building in public plus lead magnets
chunks.text:
- Output: 500k-1M views per week. Two building-in-public accounts (his and his co-founder's), plus ~8 accounts total including employees and family "satellite" accounts posting lead-magnet content daily.
- Method: find the posts getting the most engagement on LinkedIn, adapt to your niche, post. Images made with ChatGPT. Tie viral topics (e.g. Claude Cowork) to the product.
- Lead magnet flow: people comment, he replies with the guide link; the same guide is reused in cold email. Example: a lead-magnet post with ~12,000 views.
- Satellite accounts like, comment and share each post to give the initial boost. He feeds each account's network daily by connecting with new people through GojiBerry.
- Funnel: post, lead magnet, profile visit, free trial, customer. Profile tips: "visit my website" link, clean photo, banner.

chunks.heading: Growing on X
chunks.text:
- Two accounts (his and his co-founder's). He was inactive for 6 months, then posted 1-3 times a day. Reported 6M+ impressions in a year, 51k profile visits, 50k+ website visitors, all free.
- Follower hack: list the tools you use, find their founders on X, and publish genuine posts about how those tools helped your company. "Founders love free marketing." A post tagging a large SaaS account (300k+ followers) got retweeted and brought 100-500 followers at once.
- After that: follow and interact with good creators, then build in public with actionable proof, not just numbers (e.g. "I did this, I got that"). Tag the biggest players so they retweet.
- Content mix: promotional-with-value, lead magnet (a "course" comment post drew 300+ comments), and journey posts. Pinned post got 29,000 views and 3,000+ site clicks.
- Articles get strong reach. He pays for the top Premium plan (~$50-60/month), saying you won't go viral on the free plan. Posts are drafted by voice-noting ChatGPT. He recommends one X account per co-founder.

chunks.heading: Reddit and YouTube SEO
chunks.text:
- Reddit: 30M+ impressions, 13M+ views cited elsewhere, hundreds of customers; helps SEO, backlinks and LLM visibility. Top posts 100k-200k views.
- Warm-up: join niche subreddits (SaaS, MicroSaaS, Startup Ideas). Days 1-7 only upvote (~50/day); days 8-14 only comment (~50/day) with no links; then post one post without a link, then one with a small link 5 days later, then everywhere with proof.
- Posts: long storytelling with proof (e.g. "I paid five influencers on LinkedIn to promote my SaaS", "Rejected from Y Combinator", ranking #1 on Product Hunt). Every marketing win becomes a post. "If you try to promote, it's not going to work. You always need to entertain."
- Process: voice-chat the story to ChatGPT (often in French), translate and format. Post 3x per week on 12 subreddits with the same post and a tweaked title. Friends upvote, targeting 10 upvotes fast.
- Moderation: ban haters rather than argue. He's been banned 3-4 times; recreate accounts on a different browser. No VPN or proxies.
- YouTube SEO: make ~5-minute review videos on competitors (e.g. "PhantomBuster 2026 review"): thumbnail with his face over their site screenshot, walk through features and pricing, then "there is an alternative" and pitch GojiBerry. Some videos drive hundreds of views from people searching the competitor's name. Advice: map all competitors and rank on each.

chunks.heading: B2B influencer marketing
chunks.text:
- Find influencers by searching LinkedIn for your niche keywords and seeing who gets traction.
- Offer: he writes the post, builds the lead magnet and visual; the influencer posts and replies to every comment with the guide link and software. He only does one format, viral lead-magnet posts (no videos, no point-of-view posts).
- Price: $300-$800 per post, usually about $500, which can bring $1,000-$3,000 in ARR. Negotiation tactic: if they ask for more, trade by adding posts (e.g. $1,000 for two posts). Ask the influencer to introduce friends. He keeps a pool of 5-10 influencers, working with them every 2 weeks.
- Rules: resource must be sent in comments, not DMs (visible proof, and non-commenters can still click). Don't pay upfront on the first deal; pay once it's live. Ask for proof and impressions of recent posts.
- Vetting: check the comments. The same people liking, or AI-generated comments, means bad. Fake-engagement influencers brought no visitors; a good one (Eric) delivered about 1,000 site visitors per post.
- Agencies save time but cost about twice as much per influencer.

chunks.heading: Demos, routing and Meta ads
chunks.text:
- Demos: 5-8 per day, could get ~20. All content, outreach and ads push a blueprint, and the blueprint pushes a booking link. He took all demos himself, which crowds out marketing: three hours of content can drive 50 customers versus 5-8 calls converting 4-6.
- Calendly routing: not an ICP match gets the blueprint or group demo; small teams (0-5 salespeople) get a webinar or blueprint ("for 99.9% of teams, you don't actually need a demo"); only big teams book a call. He's hiring two salespeople plus a freelancer.
- Demo style: don't sell. Ask what they want to achieve, show the product step by step, show results. Close with the 7-day free trial ("you will not spend $1 before knowing that it works"). Demo-to-trial rate is 70%.
- Meta ads: spy on SaaS competitors' ads in the Meta ad library, copy and adapt them. Static ads and memes via ChatGPT, UGC via Arcads, some agency video. Runs 67 ads, retargeting plus lookalike acquisition campaigns, pixel on the site and a Stripe webhook to track trials.
- Numbers: ~€7,000 (~$9,000) spent last month, under 10% of revenue. Retargeting cost about €91 per trial, ~35% trial-to-customer, so ~€270 per customer versus ~€400 LTV; one day showed €75 per trial and another €6 (possible winner). Goal: scale to €3,000-10,000/day at the same cost per result.

chunks.heading: Plan from $1M to $10M ARR
chunks.text:
- Scalable levers: influencer marketing (the one he thinks unlocks 1 to 10), higher ad budget, affiliate program (30% lifetime commission, already ~$40,000), more SEO, and content on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram.
- Non-scalable: his own X and LinkedIn posting; grows but isn't predictable.
- Sales: two salespeople so more slots open and he can focus on scalable work.
- Hires: product manager, growth, developer, head of customer support at roughly $70k each (~$280k/year), plus sales.
- Product: add email and WhatsApp (multi-channel) and more AI features. He expects $1M to $3M in about 3 months; $3M to $10M "will take way more time".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn Czerny, CMO of Gojiberry, walks through each growth phase from 0 to $3.2M ARR: selling manually before building, spamming Reddit, then industrializing LinkedIn lead magnets and paid B2B influencers. He also covers card-required trials, ads economics and what YC changed.

chunks.heading: Positioning: Gojiberry as the cheap link between intent signals and outreach
chunks.text:
- Romàn is CMO of Gojiberry, a B2B lead-gen SaaS. It started as "signals only": enter your website and it lists leads in your niche showing buying intent.
- User interviews showed customers had lead lists but didn't know what to do with them, so outreach (LinkedIn, email) was added. That kept users returning and let them test whether the leads were any good.
- The earlier SaaS, Cocoi (e-commerce/Klaviyo/SMS marketing), was 100% outreach. Romàn found e-merchants by searching LinkedIn and closed them in demos, which led to selling intent-based lead lists.
- He treats "best data" as a non-claim: Apollo and similar tools all say it. "Intent data" was a hot topic in the US, and the promise of "contact high-intent leads" translates to "we bring you business".
- His thesis on red oceans: "if it's a red ocean, it means that there is business, and if there is business, if you are seen, well you simply take the business."
- Competitor gap: tools did signals or outreach, rarely both. One good competitor, Autom-style, charged about $600/month for its cheapest plan; Gojiberry's $99 made it accessible.
- Product direction: weekly new signals and AI features (chat that builds campaigns, near-automatic replies). He wants a "collective brain" where data across all customers shows which lead types respond to which offers (for example, growth managers respond 3x more than sales managers).

chunks.heading: Pricing, trial and funnel structure
chunks.text:
- Self-serve plan: $99/month, includes 2 LinkedIn seats, with credits for extra emails/phone numbers. Mostly solo users and small teams (PLG).
- Teams segment (5+ seats): 2-week to 1-month pilot, a shared Slack channel, then quarterly or annual contracts. Harder to crack, but bigger tickets and longer retention.
- Price never changed from $99; the offer was tested heavily instead.
- Trial: 7 days, card required. Reasons: costs from API/enrichment abuse, and it filters out non-serious users. Personally he would skip the trial and charge $99 directly.
- A/B test of a $1 trial vs free trial (card required): the free trial earned more despite more users and removed fake/temporary cards.
- About 20% of site traffic is from India, with very few paying customers there.
- Trial-to-paid conversion is about 40%. He attributes it to the card on file plus near-immediate leads, since users stay engaged waiting for replies.
- Funnel: every lead magnet has a "book a call" button. Small teams go to a near-daily webinar; large teams go to a sales call (Romàn or the sales rep). Big names (Qonto, Revolut, HubSpot, Nokia) often appear as a solo signup who then brings colleagues, after which a head of department asks to talk.

chunks.heading: Growth by phase: $0 to 10k MRR via manual outreach and selling before building
chunks.text:
- Earlier Gojiberry versions had failed twice. For v3, Romàn told his developer to stop coding until the need was validated: "Sell the solution, and then as soon as you sell it, we start coding it."
- He sold manually with a crude 6-slide PowerPoint: $99/month for 100 leads with purchase intent. He found the leads himself on LinkedIn for an afternoon per customer, which taught him how the product would work.
- Tools: Walaxy (scrape people who liked relevant LinkedIn posts, run sequences), Instantly (email) with pre-warmed domains. Never use your own or brand-new domains.
- Message was a simple "I can help you get better leads, let's talk". Several demos a day.
- Pricing tests: sometimes 500 leads for $500/month, 100 for $100/month.
- Demo-to-paid conversion was about 70%, helped by a money-back guarantee if the leads didn't fit.
- Delegating lead-finding to Fiverr freelancers was a disaster. He closed the agency and moved to the tool.
- His advice: if starting from scratch, do outreach first, because you can launch in 2 days and test the offer.

chunks.heading: Reddit: $10k to $25k MRR
chunks.text:
- He ran about 10 accounts with proxies, posting in about 50 SaaS subreddits a day. Workflow: voice-talk stories to ChatGPT (how he sold his old SaaS, how to find leads), turn them into long posts, change titles per subreddit, drop the product link inside valuable posts.
- Friends boosted posts. He hit the top of SaaS categories, with days of about 5,000 visitors. Of 5,000 visitors, roughly 10 to 20 became customers.
- Reddit leads booked more calls than LinkedIn leads, as they needed more trust-building.
- Totals: about 300,000 to 400,000 visitors and over 14 million views in 6 months, at no ad cost.
- Downsides: very aggressive toward self-promotion, banned accounts, brand nickname "Spamberry", harassment (fake calendar bookings, parasitic SEO threads like "Gojiberry got my LinkedIn banned" that rank on Google). Reddit users are not the best buyers; heads of sales don't browse there.
- He says it is now much harder than when he did it. A gentler route he suggests: distribute lead magnets without your brand name. His verdict: worth it to test how an idea is received and how the site converts.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn lead magnets with Claude: $25k to about $250k MRR
chunks.text:
- He noticed "comment 'Claude'" posts getting 3,000 to 5,000 comments. Since Gojiberry uses Claude in its backend, he made Claude-themed lead magnets, for example "how to book more appointments with Claude", where the resource pushes Gojiberry.
- Results: 2,000 comments per post, 1,000 to 3,000 MRR per post; posts sometimes reach 200,000 views. ARR went from about 1M to almost 3M largely from this.
- Lead magnet page structure: founder intro, a demo video of the tool, a playbook explaining why intent data beats generic lists, how to find leads with Gojiberry, templates, a book-a-call button, case studies. Effectively a sales page.
- Metric: "The more lead magnets you distribute, the more MRR you bring in."
- Operations: 3 lead magnets per day across 3 accounts, a new magnet weekly, a French account reusing the same structure. He manages all team accounts on X and LinkedIn.
- All three founder profiles and the company page got banned from LinkedIn 2 days before the recording, a typical outcome for outreach tools. He notes few channels are truly owned.

chunks.heading: Buying LinkedIn influencer posts
chunks.text:
- About 100+ influencers: about 50 managed by Romàn, 50 via the agency Obvious (about 20 posts/month, fixed monthly price).
- Sourcing method 1: approach accounts with strong traction who don't run lead magnets, saying "I'm looking to buy posts". Offer lower figures, but Gojiberry writes everything and pays upfront.
- Method 2: search "Claude" in the LinkedIn search bar, find lead-magnet posts, ask for a post "exactly like this one" and negotiate.
- Execution: give the influencer the post word for word plus the image, and have them reply to every comment with the magnet link.
- Pricing: small freelancers about $200 to $250 per post, often with outsized engagement; $500 for established or ambassador accounts. Sweet spot was $250 to $500. Executive-level accounts cost more but reach big companies.
- Pay-per-click alternative: nano.xyz at about €2 per highly qualified click (limited supply since competitors joined).
- Tracking: a simple Excel sheet of who posts each week, what content was prepared, and whether it performs. Keep what performs, stop and revisit the rest.
- He says very few companies pay LinkedIn influencers, so deals are easy, and the value is huge: a $1,000 to $10,000 post can equal 2.5 to 3 signed clients in LTV.

chunks.heading: Meta ads, X and AI usage
chunks.text:
- Ads are about 10% of traffic, roughly €2,000/day, run by an outsourced friend. Creative is UGC, mostly a creator holding up the product. UGC agency results were inconclusive on TikTok, but the UGC works in ads.
- Unit economics: trial cost about €96; with 40% trial-to-paid, customer acquisition cost about €230 to €240. LTV about €500 after one year, so around 2x and profitable within about a month and a half. He notes ads cash is advanced and platform-dependent, and ad tracking is unmeasured (no attribution tool). Impressions also help demos and other channels.
- X: posts only in English, follows only US/UK accounts, long voice-to-GPT posts, lead magnets, videos and launches. One video reached 800,000 views and gave about 1,000 subscribers. Not the biggest revenue channel but a stable audience. Accounts he follows: Tibo Maker, Marc Lou, an Origami competitor, and others.
- Current numbers: ARR $3.2M, MRR about €235,000 to €236,000.
- AI use: ChatGPT voice for posts, GPT image generation for visuals, a note-taker for sales calls that drafts follow-up emails, Cursor to build his own Chrome extensions for LinkedIn automation (previously a five-figure developer cost). In the product, AI qualifies and scores leads, writes personalized messages and orders outreach hottest first.

chunks.heading: Y Combinator and fundraising
chunks.text:
- He finished YC a week before recording. He is CMO, his partner Pierre Elliot is CEO and pitched at demo day.
- The cost is 7%, and he calls it worth it "a billion times": network, mindset shift (from "sell at 100M" to a much bigger ambition), and mentorship from people who sold companies for $300M to $600M or IPO'd.
- Mechanics: 3 months, biweekly goals reported to a small group, partner one-on-ones, talks from Sam Altman and Airbnb's co-founder. They worked 18 hours a day in a San Francisco house. He is convinced they would never have gone from 1M to 3.2M in 3 months otherwise.
- The YC logo makes selling in the US much easier. YC also gave over $2M in AI tokens.
- Raise: gave up 10% for $4M on a SAFE capped at $40M, total dilution 17% (83% retained). Investors came to them via demo day, with money arriving quickly. They converted to a US entity; the French company is inactive.
- Plan: spend the $4M on product, go-to-market help and ads, or choose between a Series A and a cash-flowing business. Advice: spend at least 10 days in San Francisco (use Luma to find events, especially Y Combinator-linked ones).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn Czerny explains why Ecom French Touch sells low-priced, frequently repurchased info products backed by proof of its own results. He covers how the team grew a 25k-member Facebook group, then moved the audience to YouTube and Telegram, and what the PayPal freeze taught him about diversifying.

chunks.heading: From 5-Euro Freelancing to a 25,000-Member Community
chunks.text:
Romàn Czerny started out as a freelancer on 5-euro platforms while studying engineering. He sold services there, then PDFs in an automated way, before telling himself "I'm selling my time."

- He spent months observing what buyers wanted and what could be recurring without human intervention.
- He ended up among the platform's top sellers with well-crafted PDFs.
- He then offered this method to clients, and later launched Ecom French Touch with Maxime.
- For him, betting on a recognized skill starts with freelancing or "done for you." Selling your time at the beginning is normal: "you have to start somewhere."

chunks.heading: Why Sell Low-Priced Products With High Recurrence
chunks.text:
Romàn thinks that five years ago, he could have sold his content for 500 to 1000 euros. Today, the market has changed.

- Buyers of training courses got "slaughtered" by expensive, bad products, back when "you could sell any PDF for 500 bucks." They lost trust.
- Ecom French Touch therefore offers very low prices (17 euros per month for the training of the month, with no subscription) with a high repeat-purchase rate. This restores customers' trust, and they apply what they learn and get results.
- A cheap product means low commitment: the customer expects little, so you can give them an experience that exceeds their expectations.
- A buyer from a year ago is very often still a buyer.
- He considers the opposite view short-termist: a seller who collects 500,000 euros with 1000-euro courses would, in his view, have made far more by selling cheaper with recurrence over the following years. He acknowledges that some expensive products are excellent, but that is not his model.
- He cannot justify a high price for videos, because someone who does nothing with them gets nothing. He only sells coaching at a high price, where he can transform a business ("x5, x10 or x20") and "give a kick in the pants" when needed.
- His value ladder: low-priced training to get started and get results, then coaching, which is more specific and more human.

chunks.heading: Selling on Proof Rather Than Curiosity
chunks.text:
Curiosity sells cheap products, but Romàn does not rely on it.

- The positioning rests on their own results: "everything we sell, we can prove 100%."
- Proof cited: a Facebook group grown from 0 to 25,000 members, a Telegram group, a YouTube channel with over 100,000 subscribers.
- The second pillar is customer recurrence. He says nobody on the market offers better for this price, and that is their credo.

chunks.heading: The Facebook Hack That Launched the Community
chunks.text:
At the start, Facebook let you add thousands of people from competing groups with one click.

- You joined groups in the topic area with your profile and added the members as friends, then into your group. The next day, about half accepted.
- When the groups were exhausted, they moved on to pages via Facebook graph search, for example a page with 120,000 fans, to invite everyone.
- To scale up, they bought the equivalent of 200 Facebook accounts, used three computers, and coded scripts that crawled through the groups and added everyone automatically.
- The groups' audiences overlapped, so they ended up covering most of the niche's audience. This gave a base to launch the YouTube channel: a thousand subscribers from the first video.
- Facebook closed this loophole after about two months of use. Insurance groups were already offering them one euro per member added, and they estimated they could earn several thousand euros a day. He says that with a two-year head start they would be "very, very rich."
- In his view, this is no longer possible today and he has no desire to do it again.

chunks.heading: Keeping the Community: Value and Engagement
chunks.text:
The hack is not enough, he repeated. With 50,000 people in another niche, "I'd crash."

- What worked: giving enormous value and having a very active community manager. On Facebook, they reply to everyone in the group. They added lives and plenty of resources.
- Result: only three or four members out of 25,000 complained about being added, and people stayed loyal.
- The group became the biggest marketing/dropshipping/e-commerce group on Facebook, which recommends it first for those searches.

chunks.heading: Multi-Platform: One Platform at a Time, Then Audience Transfer
chunks.text:
Romàn describes each channel as serving a different type of audience.

- YouTube: the most formal, almost no interaction; you deliver content and that's it.
- Facebook: community, with answers to every question.
- Telegram: close to texting, more intimate, with behind-the-scenes of the business.
- Advice: choose one platform and saturate it, then transfer the audience. Starting from zero on a platform is very hard. With a base, for example 200 fans on Instagram, the algorithm starts pushing you. In his view, you could open Snapchat or another network and get people by announcing it to the existing community.
- Choose the platform closest to your "zone of genius": YouTube if you're good at video, Facebook if you're good at community management, Telegram if you prefer quick exchanges. He can make YouTube and Facebook explode, but says he is unable to do anything on Twitter.

chunks.heading: The Udemy Hack: Free, Reviews, Then Paid, With Lead Capture
chunks.text:
Romàn put all his programs on Udemy, reluctantly (he dislikes their pricing policy), but he feels that an extra 200 to 300 euros in monthly revenue is not something to turn down.

- Put a free course on the platform.
- Post it everywhere, in every group, announcing that it becomes paid in two days. Ask people to leave a good review.
- Once it's well ranked with reviews, switch it to the price you want. The platform promotes it and it generates revenue.
- Free enrollees are also leads to collect. He says he can easily gather 1000 emails this way, and has used this method several times.

chunks.heading: The Bold Move With a Footballer (Djibril Cissé)
chunks.text:
One evening, while looking at Patrice Evra's account (2.8 million followers), who was selling a nutrition ebook, Romàn concluded that footballers selling programs are obvious targets.

- He sent voice messages to footballers: France national team players, Ligue 1 stars, Benzema. Two minutes later, Djibril Cissé replied with his number.
- On the phone, he said Evra had released a product and that he was offering to do better. Cissé invited him to his home the next day.
- He spent the night on a PowerPoint, showed up, presented, and Cissé accepted. He could present with confidence because the subject (sales funnels, marketing) is his field.
- Contract signed, sales funnel built, launch of Cissé's fitness program: a success, even though they had expected more media coverage.
- Lesson: he proved he can put together a project overnight with a big name.

chunks.heading: Failure and Diversification: The PayPal Freeze
chunks.text:
Romàn cites his hardest ordeal: PayPal froze about 30,000 euros after a spike in volume in a single day, for 90 to 180 days (he doesn't remember exactly).

- The company was just starting out, they had to pay charges and taxes on money that wasn't available, and 50% of customers paid via PayPal.
- Support was ineffective: he even contacted a manager via LinkedIn, without result, because the decision came from California.
- Lessons applied since: diversify networks, payment processors and payment systems, have two accounts, two email sending addresses, a lawyer for the terms and conditions and legal matters, and always have a backup plan before launching.
- He advises not depending on PayPal.

chunks.heading: Work and Mindset
chunks.text:
- "You get nothing for nothing": results come from enormous work, even if online business makes access easier.
- He gets bored quickly, needs new challenges, and works in sessions of a few days on one subject.
- His motto: perseverance, "God helps those who help themselves." He refuses certain practices that don't fit his code of conduct.
- You can make money on the internet without advertising, and it has become the easiest path.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn's playbook from scaling two SaaS (Coco AI to €500k ARR, now Gojiberry AI): validate with real conversations before coding, build one feature, match competitor pricing, and win the first 10 customers manually. Growth then comes from high-intent LinkedIn outreach, Reddit, cold email on fresh signals, and cheap compounding channels like free tools, blog, directories and YouTube.

chunks.heading: From idea to first demand: validate before building
chunks.text:
- Romàn says launching a SaaS without validating the idea is a "costly gamble". Validation confirms real demand, saves time and money, and shapes the concept before full development.
- His validation toolkit: customer interviews and surveys, landing pages or pre-sales to gauge willingness to pay, Reddit and community feedback, competitor analysis, an MVP or beta, free trials, and Product Hunt launches.
- He tried two ideas for his second SaaS. The first was an AI note taker. It had a landing page and email signups, so he built it, but it didn't sell. It was "too complex too early", so he pivoted before going further. The second was a GTM platform to get leads and do outreach, which became Gojiberry AI.
- He found the need to pivot by talking to prospects. He calls building without talking to people the classic founder mistake.
- The strongest signal is people ready to give a credit card before a single line of code is written. A good early test is posting on Reddit to see whether people will pay.
- No developer is needed at this stage.
- His action plan:
  1. List ideas.
  2. Build a very simple landing page.
  3. Find potential customers to talk to.
  4. If they're ready to pay by the end of the call, he treats that as the sign he's on the right track.
- He notes a SaaS takes several years, so "choose your battles wisely".

chunks.heading: Building the product: partners, one feature, no contracts too early
chunks.text:
- A solo marketer can hire a developer or team up with a CTO. Romàn has always preferred a CTO partner. Hiring developers is expensive, a co-founder is far more invested, and the right partner "is worth ten developers". The trade-off is owning only 50% when selling the company.
- A solo developer is "a jackpot", but teaming with a marketer helps growth and lets the developer stay in their zone of genius.
- He avoids dev agencies. He imagines a bug on a Saturday afternoon and an agency that only replies on Monday. His ideal is an in-house developer reachable anytime.
- He found the Gojiberry AI developer through a referral from his network. He also recommends posting in startup and incubator groups.
- He advises not signing anything before the first euros come in. Build an MVP, launch a landing page, and see if you can work together. "Focus on traction first, the paperwork can wait."
- He wants one feature at the start. Never build a feature unless you are 100% sure it will increase retention, improve customer results, or grow revenue. Build one feature, sell it, see results, then iterate.

chunks.heading: Pricing: match competitors first, then test
chunks.text:
- Romàn says there is no magic formula apart from testing. Early on, he aligns pricing with competitors, because they are already selling at that price and the audience is comfortable paying it. He has done this with every SaaS he has launched.
- This gives initial cash flow, and he adjusts later based on results.
- Gojiberry AI pricing history:
  - At first he took only demos and showed no pricing on the landing page.
  - He then tested 499, 297, 199 and 99.
  - At 497 he could sell, but customers churned quickly.
  - At 297 he sold more, but it required calls and manual sales.
  - He now sells only at $99/month with a 7-day free trial, mostly self-serve.
- He describes pricing as a constant process of testing and adjusting.

chunks.heading: Getting the first 10 customers
chunks.text:
- Romàn says the first ten customers give the confidence to keep going. As with Y Combinator and successful SaaS founders, there is no magic formula: "you have to grind for them".
- Sources include friends' introductions, phone calls, manual LinkedIn DMs, and cold emails. The goal is 20 to 30 meetings and closing ten of them. "Try everything you can."
- For Gojiberry AI, he did LinkedIn outreach from his personal account, "sending messages like crazy". He offered a demo to everyone who replied. A small slide deck converted them to paying customers. He built the deck in 15 minutes and calls it "VERY basic".
- Any method is valid if it gets people on calls. Don't accept "I'm interested, but maybe later". By the end of the call you want "Okay, let's do it". You can then say either "We're currently building it" or "you can start today".

chunks.heading: Support and customer success
chunks.text:
- Add a small chat bubble to the site. Gojiberry AI uses Crisp, and he says free alternatives exist.
- With early customers, schedule quick calls at day 7 and day 15. Ask:
  - Which parts of the product do you use?
  - What do you like or dislike?
  - Would you leave a review?
  - Would you recommend us?
- Gojiberry AI offers review calls to every client. Romàn says most people don't do this.
- Keeping a customer is much easier than acquiring one. Keep support fast and communication easy, and check in proactively with your best users.
- "When someone decides to leave your product, it's already too late." Spot signs of churn earlier.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn high-intent outreach (about 25% of sales)
chunks.text:
- Romàn gets about 25% of Gojiberry AI sales from LinkedIn outreach because he targets warm leads.
- Cold outreach, per his figures: 1-2% response rate, about 100 messages per meeting, and defensive prospects.
- High-intent outreach: 25-40% response rate, about 10 messages per meeting, and prospects who are active in the market.
- A comment like "interested" is a raised hand, which he calls "a 100x stronger signal than any data point you can buy".
- A high-intent lead is someone showing signals right now, not just an ICP on paper. Signals include:
  - Liking or commenting on competitor posts
  - A new role or key hires
  - Fresh funding
  - Following relevant influencers or hashtags
  - Publicly sharing pain points
- Doing this manually takes 5+ hours a day, so he uses AI agents. Gojiberry agents cover competitor profiles, influencer profiles, recent job changers, the top 5% of ICP, recent fundraises, LinkedIn engagement, interactions with your company, and profile visits. Company page visits, page followers and hiring signals are listed as coming soon.
- He says one agent search produced 300 high-intent leads in a week.
- Message sequence (short, no pitch):
  - Initial DM (23 words): "Hey [Name], Quick question - what's your biggest challenge with [topic] right now?" He says 80% answer.
  - Meeting DM (after a reply): "Interesting - we just solved that exact problem for [similar company]. Mind if I send you a 3-minute video showing how?" He says 60% say yes. He then records a Loom covering their challenge, a similar client case study, his approach, and a soft CTA.
  - Backup DM if no response: "Hey [Name], did you get a chance to check my message above? Noticed you're [specific observation] - we should chat."
- His AI prompts: a research prompt (biggest challenge, current project, a genuine compliment, under 50 words), a writing prompt (30-word DM that sounds like texting a friend, one simple question, no sales language, no exclamation points), and a follow-up prompt (25 words acknowledging their situation with social proof).
- Mindset: treat LinkedIn as "a warm lead generation machine". "Every post is a net. Every comment is a lead."

chunks.heading: Reddit as an inbound channel
chunks.text:
- Reasons he gives for Reddit in 2025:
  - 97.2M daily active users in 2024, up 47% year on year.
  - Google paid $60M for exclusive indexing rights, so Reddit mentions help SEO.
  - About 40% of AI-generated answers reference Reddit, so mentions help LLM visibility.
- Finding subreddits:
  - Start with SaaS-friendly subs.
  - Follow where active authors post elsewhere.
  - Go niche by industry, using a ChatGPT prompt for 10 relevant subreddits.
  - Search competitor mentions to see where they're discussed.
- Commenting rules to avoid bans:
  - Give more than you take, and mention the product only when it's the natural solution.
  - Be careful with links. Mention the product by name, share a link only if asked, and never reuse the same linked comment across threads.
  - Balance promo with genuine contributions. Max 15 comments/day per account, under 50% promotional. Spread volume across accounts and avoid VPNs.
  - Warm up first. Get at least 10 karma before mentioning the SaaS. At 10 karma do 3-4 mentions/day, and at 20 karma scale to 6-7/day.
- Measuring: use Yandex.Metrica (free, with Webvisor session replay). Run an experiment of about 20 mentions/day for 3 days, pause 3 days (traffic peaks in 1-2 days then fades), analyze visits, signups and conversion, then compare subreddit groups week by week.
- His own routine for Gojiberry AI: 7 new posts a week, each reposted in 10+ subreddits (about 70 posts/week), plus 35 SEO comments a week.
- Four formats that work:
  - Storytelling (90% value, 10% subtle mention)
  - Case studies (e.g. "403 demos in 60 days")
  - AMA threads
  - Comparisons/alternatives (e.g. "Instantly alternatives"), which are evergreen and rank on Google and LLMs
- Keyword method: seed 20-30 buyer-intent keywords, search `site:reddit.com` plus the keyword, qualify threads by traffic, recency and sub rules, then track Keyword, URL, Angle, Date, Views in a sheet. Threads that already rank for years give free compounding exposure.
- He writes posts by dictating to ChatGPT and asking it to format for Reddit. He also turns strong Reddit comments into blog posts and links back.
- Conversion funnel: posts and SEO comments, then replies/DMs with a diagnostic question ("What's your main lead source right now?"), then a resource, then a demo CTA, then a live-signals demo to close. He reports a 30-40% close rate.
- Scaling safely: always disclose your brand ("I build Gojiberry AI"), keep one account for posts and one for SEO comments, and do posting and replying manually. Vote manipulation, mass DMs and fake reviews are forbidden.

chunks.heading: Cold email on real-time intent leads
chunks.text:
- Romàn's central claim: the number one reason cold email fails is the lead source, not copy or deliverability. Static databases like Apollo and CSVs go stale, so he emails real-time high-intent leads from LinkedIn activity. At equal volume he says this gives 3-5x more replies.
- His results: about 5,000/day (~150,000/month), roughly a 2.5% reply rate, 70% of SaaS growth from outbound, and 400+ demos in 2 months without ads.
- Flow: LinkedIn signal, then Gojiberry, then enrichment, then Instantly, then Slack/CRM, then reply handling. He uses Instantly because it works from 100 to 50,000/day, has inbox placement tests and rotates domains and inboxes. He says it has been the most reliable past 5,000/day.
- Deliverability setup:
  - Buy several domains close to the brand (e.g. trygojiberry.com, getgojiberry.ai), with 3 inboxes per domain.
  - Start at 5-10/day/inbox and raise by 5-10% a day. After about 3 weeks, 20-30/day/inbox.
  - Set SPF, DKIM and DMARC, keep bounces under 2%, and cap at 30/day/inbox.
  - Run inbox placement tests (target above 80%) and pause if results go red.
- Scaling roadmap:
  - 1 domain × 3 inboxes: about 500/month
  - 5 domains × 15 inboxes: about 15k/month
  - 10 domains × 50 inboxes: about 45k/month
- Ten intent signals: engaging with a competitor's post, a new role, funding, a job post, event registration, downloading competitor content, repeat visits to your LinkedIn profile, commenting on your CEO's post, migrating away from a tool, and posting publicly about a pain point. He says signal-based timing is the difference between 0.5% and 3% reply rates.
- Copy rules:
  - Subject: 4-7 words, natural, personalized.
  - Opener: reference the exact trigger, not "Hope you are well".
  - Body: about 140 words, simple sentences, one idea per paragraph, with proof such as numbers and similar clients.
  - Personalization: use real context, with two or more layers.
  - CTA: one clear, easy step, such as a five-minute chat.
- Sequence: first email gives value and context, day 3 a soft reminder, day 7 proof or case study, day 10 break-up. Three to four touches max.
- Tested subject lines: "About your new role at {{company}}", "Quick idea for {{company}}", "Noticed this about {{competitor}}".
- Targeting: start tight, e.g. CEO / Head of Growth / Demand Gen, SaaS, 5-50 employees, US/EU, seed to Series B. Expand only after consistent results, and track ICP segments separately.
- Track weekly: emails sent, open %, reply %, positive reply %, demos booked, and results by signal type.

chunks.heading: Secondary channels: LinkedIn content, free tools, blog, directories, YouTube
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn inbound content: he posts daily, sending people to a resource or the website. He copies structures that already perform, adapting them to his style. He says attribution is hard to measure, but it reliably opens new DM opportunities.
- Free tools: build simple tools in a few hours that attract the ideal audience, who can then try the product. Gojiberry AI built several, such as a free outreach message analyser, which drive a lot of traffic. He isn't sure how much they have converted, but they boosted overall website traffic.
- Blog: publish one article a week and check which get the most impressions and clicks, then improve those. He talks to ChatGPT about what he wants to say, asks it to format the text, and publishes. He says it brings some traffic but "is not what will make your business take off". It is a good habit to start before 10K MRR.
- AI directories: listing the SaaS in 100+ AI directories takes two to three hours. It is often free and can bring a few dozen users per day, sometimes high-quality paying ones.
- YouTube: he calls it excellent, with great demos booked. The strategy is long-tail, SEO-ranked videos that drive people to the website or Calendly. He records with ScreenStudio, doesn't edit, and makes thumbnails with ChatGPT. Some videos passed 1,000 views. Videos can be reused in lead magnets and on Reddit, and they build trust through seeing his face.

chunks.heading: Benchmarks, rollout plan and first 48 hours
chunks.text:
- Y Combinator's "magic formula", as Romàn cites it: €10,000 MRR from 100 customers paying €100/month. For him, €10,000 MRR is where you know the product is scalable and demand is real.
- His track record: Coco AI (WhatsApp automation for Shopify) scaled to €500,000 ARR before he sold it because the team wasn't the right fit to take it further. Gojiberry AI is his second run at the same milestone.
- His four-week rollout, with his expected results:
  - Week 1: set up agents and sync leads to CRM, then start warm conversations. Expect 50-100 leads and 10-15 conversations.
  - Week 2: review which signals work, adjust filters, run LinkedIn and email campaigns. Expect 100-150 leads, 25-30 conversations, 5-8 calls.
  - Week 3: activate more agents and push multi-channel outreach. Expect 300-400 leads, 40-50 conversations, 10-15 calls.
  - Week 4 on: signals keep compounding into pipeline.
- First 48 hours:
  - Activate the first agents.
  - Sync leads into the outreach tool the next morning.
  - Start connecting with everyone who just showed a buying signal.
  - Follow up within 24 hours.
  - On day 2, re-engage non-responders and push for call booking.
- He claims you will book a first meeting within 7 days.
- His tool stack: Gojiberry (leads), Instantly (email), Fathom (call recording), Crisp (chat), ScreenStudio (video), ChatGPT (writing, prompts, thumbnails), Yandex.Metrica (Reddit tracking).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Romàn Czerny, co-founder of gojiberry.ai, lays out the Reddit system that brings him 30% of his demos. It covers picking subreddits, commenting without getting banned, measuring results with short sprints, and the post formats that work. It also explains how Reddit threads feed Google and LLM visibility.

chunks.heading: Why Romàn treats Reddit as a core distribution channel
chunks.text:
- Reddit brings Romàn about 30% of his demos for gojiberry.ai (his AI lead-intent tool). He says the other 70% comes from a separate system he points readers to.
- He frames Reddit as strategic for three reasons:
  - **Audience growth:** Reddit hit 97.2M daily active users in 2024, which he cites as 47% year-over-year growth.
  - **SEO:** he says Google paid $60M for exclusive indexing rights, so every mention of your SaaS on Reddit helps you rank.
  - **AI visibility:** Reddit is one of the most cited sources in LLMs. He cites roughly 40% of AI-generated answers referencing it, so your product can surface when people ask AI tools for recommendations.
- He says he and his team went from $0 to $1M ARR following their marketing and sales blueprint, and released a 1h20 course on it.

chunks.heading: Finding the right subreddits
chunks.text:
1. **SaaS-friendly subreddits:** start with a curated list of about 15 where founders and small teams share products, ask for feedback and find first users.
2. **Follow active conversations:** look at popular posts in big startup/product subreddits, then check where those authors post elsewhere. Smaller related communities are "hidden gems".
3. **Go niche:** if your SaaS targets an industry (finance, design, healthcare), find subreddits for that vertical, because general startup spaces won't be enough.
   - His ChatGPT prompt: "You are a professional Reddit marketing specialist. Provide me with 10 subreddits where I can naturally mention my service in comments and bring value in my niche. My service description is: [1-3 sentences]. Return only a list of the 10 most relevant subreddits."
4. **Watch competitor mentions:** search competitor names and keywords on Reddit. The subreddits where they're discussed are usually where you should show up too.

chunks.heading: Commenting rules to avoid bans
chunks.text:
Romàn says the biggest mistake is getting banned, and Reddit works because of its strict rules.

- **Give more than you take:** read the person's problem, give advice, and mention your product only when it's the natural solution. If it doesn't fit, just share expertise. This earns karma and credibility.
- **Be careful with links:**
  - Mention the product by name; curious people will Google it.
  - Share a link only if someone explicitly asks.
  - Never reuse the same linked comment across threads, even in "Drop your link" posts.
- **Balance promo with real contributions:**
  - Answer follow-ups under your own comments and contribute to non-promotional threads.
  - Rule of thumb: no more than 15 comments/day per account, with under 50% promotional.
  - For more volume, spread activity across multiple accounts.
  - Avoid VPNs, which Reddit flags.
- **Warm up the account:** get at least 10 karma before mentioning your SaaS by engaging in communities like r/SaaS, commenting on recent high-engagement threads, and building upvotes.
  - At 10 karma: 3-4 mentions/day.
  - At 20 karma: scale to 6-7 mentions/day.

chunks.heading: Measuring Reddit results with a 3-day sprint experiment
chunks.text:
Romàn says success is users and customers acquired, not comments posted. He recommends Yandex.Metrica (free) for seeing which channel brought each visitor, daily visits and conversions, and Webvisor session replay.

1. **Intensive test:** post about 20 relevant mentions per day for 3 days to trigger a visible traffic spike.
2. **Pause for 3 days:** Reddit traffic peaks within 1-2 days and then fades, so pausing isolates the impact.
3. **Analyze:** total visits and registrations, conversion rate, and Webvisor sessions.
4. **Compare subreddit groups:** week 1 on one group, week 2 on another, then double down where sign-ups are best.

Checklist: warm up the account (10+ karma, no self-promo early); pick subreddits via curated lists and competitor mentions; avoid spammy, low-engagement or competitor-promo posts; add value first and mix product mentions with pure advice; run 3-day sprints then pause.

chunks.heading: His own Reddit cadence and the post formats that work
chunks.text:
- Gojiberry's weekly output: 7 new posts, each reposted in 10+ subreddits (about 70 posts/week), plus 35 SEO comments.
- He writes posts by dictating them to ChatGPT, then asking it to format them for Reddit.
- Four formats he says always work:
  1. **Storytelling (90/10):** wins or fails with 90% pure value and a 10% subtle mention; it resonates because it's human.
  2. **Case studies:** e.g. "403 demos in 60 days", sharing process and numbers.
  3. **AMA threads:** let the community ask; builds authority and allows safe self-promotion.
  4. **Comparisons/alternatives:** e.g. "Instantly alternatives", "Best LinkedIn tools"; evergreen and rank on Google and LLMs.
- SEO comments (short, actionable, proof-based) keep compounding visibility for months.

chunks.heading: Keyword and thread research for Reddit SEO
chunks.text:
1. Build a seed list of 20-30 buyer-intent keywords from demo transcripts, competitor ads and Google Autocomplete.
2. Search Google with `site:reddit.com` plus the keyword.
3. Qualify threads by traffic, recency and subreddit rules.
4. Pick an angle: mini-case, checklist or numbers.
5. Track in a simple sheet: Keyword → URL → Angle → Date → Views.

He notes threads that have ranked for years give "free compounding exposure".

Low-key mentions that boost SEO:
- Contextual mentions, e.g. "We track 15 intent signals at Gojiberry AI; here's the checklist you can use even without our tool."
- Portable value others cite: checklists, prompts, spreadsheets.
- Interlinking: turn strong Reddit comments into blog posts and link back, so the content is indexed twice. The goal is to get the brand indexed by Google and LLMs for long-term reach.

chunks.heading: Turning Reddit conversations into sales
chunks.text:
Funnel:
- Posts and SEO comments create attention.
- Replies and DMs open with a diagnostic question: "What's your main lead source right now?"
- Offer a quick resource, then a demo CTA.
- In the demo, show live signals and close a pilot or annual plan.

Micro-scripts:
- Public: "Happy to share the 15-signal checklist → comment CHECKLIST if useful."
- DM: "Out of curiosity, what's your biggest challenge with LinkedIn lead flow?"

He says these natural conversations produce self-qualified leads with a 30-40% close rate.

chunks.heading: Scaling safely and his tool stack
chunks.text:
- **Allowed:** discovery automation, draft suggestions, engagement reminders.
- **Manual-only:** posting, replying, brand disclosure.
- **Forbidden:** vote manipulation, mass DMs, fake reviews.
- **Hygiene:** one account for posts and one for SEO comments; warm accounts with neutral activity; always disclose the brand, e.g. "I build Gojiberry AI".
- **Tool stack to close deals:** gojiberry.ai to find leads, instantly.ai to contact them, fathom.ai to record calls.
- He also references a LinkedIn high-intent outreach system that booked 12 demos in 5 days with AI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Gojiberry's essay argues Anthropic's Claude for Small Business automates back-office work on data that already exists, but leaves top-of-funnel prospecting untouched. It frames sales as two columns (before and after a lead lands in the CRM) and says the moat is moving upstream. It is also a product pitch for Gojiberry.

chunks.heading: Claude for Small Business automates the back-office, not the pipeline
chunks.text:
- On May 13, 2026, Anthropic shipped Claude for Small Business, a packaged version of Claude Cowork aimed at the 25-employee shop rather than the enterprise.
- The bundle has 15 ready-to-run workflows (finance, operations, marketing, customer service) and 15 skills that plug them into existing tools.
- Connectors include QuickBooks, PayPal, HubSpot, Canva, DocuSign, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Square, Stripe and Webflow.
- Every task is initiated by the owner and validated before anything ships, gets published or moves money. Permissions are inherited from the connected tools.
- Romàn calls it "a solid product". For a small team losing 5-10 hours a week to back-office work, he sees "a meaningful unlock".
- His view of what is new: not the technology, since Claude could do most of this for a year, but that a frontier lab is building specifically for the 25-person business. AI tooling had been priced and shaped for the enterprise for two years.
- Example workflow: scheduling payroll by reconciling the QuickBooks cash position against incoming PayPal settlements, with the owner approving the run before payment leaves the account.

chunks.heading: The gap: managing demand is not creating demand
chunks.text:
- Romàn's core distinction: "managing demand ≠ creating demand".
- The HubSpot connector does lead triage and campaign attribution on leads already in the CRM. That is useful, but he says it is not prospecting.
- His pattern across all the workflows: they operate on data that already exists in your tools (invoices in QuickBooks, leads in HubSpot, drafted contracts). Claude orchestrates what is there and does not go fetch what isn't.
- What Claude for Small Business does not do:
  - Source new prospects you've never heard of.
  - Build targeted lists from scratch.
  - Enrich prospects with verified emails and phone numbers.
  - Surface buying-intent signals from the web.
  - Run personalized outreach at scale across channels.
- Keeping the top of the funnel filled week after week is, in his words, the hardest part for a small team, and it is still entirely on the owner.

chunks.heading: Why Anthropic left prospecting alone
chunks.text:
Romàn calls this a deliberate, sensible choice by Anthropic, for three reasons:

- **Governance:** outbound prospecting touches deliverability, compliance, GDPR and opt-in rules. A mistake means brand damage and blacklisted inboxes.
- **Trust threshold:** paying a payroll bill is one binary action. Reaching out to 500 net-new contacts is 500 micro-actions, each needing judgment.
- **Horizontal product:** Claude is a general agent, not a vertical sales engine. Prospecting is a vertical with its own data plumbing, scoring logic and intent signals.

His conclusion is that Anthropic shipped the safe, defensible layer. The prospecting layer performs very differently when built as a specialized tool than when bolted onto a horizontal agent.

chunks.heading: Why the launch matters: validation and the next 12-24 months
chunks.text:
- Romàn argues the real news is validation: a lab that ships enterprise infrastructure now treats SMB agentic automation as a real, mature market.
- Adoption data he cites (SBA Office of Advocacy, via tech press): the AI usage gap between large enterprises and SMBs closed from 1.8x to 1.2x between early 2024 and August 2025.
- His prediction: if the back-office is being automated now, AI ownership of the pipeline is next, "Not in 2030. In the next 12-24 months."
- SMBs that wait will be prospecting by hand against competitors whose AI already fills their top of funnel.
- He compares it to earlier cycles, each of which went from specialized tooling to mainstream adoption to a gap between early and late adopters:
  - Email marketing, 2010-2015.
  - CRM, 2015-2020.
  - Cold outreach automation, 2020-2024.

chunks.heading: Playbook: what a small sales team should do this quarter
chunks.text:
1. **Make two columns.**
   - Right column: everything after a lead lands in the CRM (qualification, attribution, follow-up sequencing, deal stage updates, reporting). This is increasingly automated by tools like Claude, so plan for it.
   - Left column: everything before a lead lands in the CRM (list building, intent signal monitoring, enrichment, cold outreach, reply handling). This is "still 100% your responsibility" and is where the leverage lives.
2. **Build prospecting first, not last.**
   - Most small teams build in the wrong order: CRM, then sequencing tool, then "we'll figure out prospecting later". He says "later" is the bottleneck.
   - If the post-lead workflow gets automated for free, the competitive moat moves up the funnel. Teams that get specialized prospecting right now get a 12-month head start.
   - He points to buying-intent signals as the starting point for this layer (he has a guide to 13 of them).
3. **Adopt the standard "you click, AI ships".**
   - A sales AI vendor that pitches full automation with no human checkpoint before outbound goes out is a red flag. He says the trust model has moved.
4. **Stop using Claude as a sales tool.**
   - He calls it an ops tool with sales-adjacent features. Use it for paperwork, reconciling numbers, drafting comms and routing contracts, and pair it with a dedicated prospecting layer for the top of the funnel. "The two work together."

chunks.heading: How Romàn positions Gojiberry against the gap
chunks.text:
- Gojiberry is described as the specialized top-of-funnel companion to the back-office automation Anthropic shipped.
- It surfaces buying signals across the web, enriches contacts with verified emails and phone numbers, and delivers warm leads weekly.
- It uses the same owner-in-the-loop trust model: you validate before anything goes out, applied to the prospecting half of revenue.
- Positioning line: "The back-office is solved. The pipeline is the open frontier."
- Content tactic in the piece: an interactive 3-question quiz (about 60 seconds, no signup) at the top of the article.
  - Questions cover where the owner's week goes, how recently the prospect list was refreshed, and what AI does in the sales stack today.
  - Results route to a "your pipeline needs its own layer" pitch or a "you're ahead, double down on signal quality" pitch.
  - CTAs repeat through the article, each with its own `utm_content` tag (cta1 to cta5) for attribution.
- Offer in the footer CTA: free trial, live in 5 minutes, cancel anytime.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A small sales team should automate in a fixed order: logging, booking, follow-up timing, signal-based targeting, then drafting. Four jobs stay human: replies, objections, pricing, and anything a bad list would multiply. The essay also gives a deliverability checklist and a 4-week plan for a 3-person team.

chunks.heading: Automate in order: cheapest and safest first, targeting fourth
chunks.text:
