- Romàn's core claim: "Automation multiplies whatever you feed it." A good sequence sent to the wrong list reaches the wrong people faster, with better follow-up.
- His example: a three-person team buys a sending tool in week one. By week three it pushes 400 emails a month at an unargued list. The sequence runs perfectly and the pipeline doesn't move, because real work was automated in the wrong order.
- He defines B2B sales automation as handing mechanical work (capturing activity, sending, scheduling, reminding, updating records) to software. Judgment stays with the human: software decides when something happens, the seller decides what it says.
- Five jobs in a seller's week: find accounts worth a message, draft a first message, chase people who went quiet, get a time on the calendar, keep the record straight.
- His five-step order: 1) log what happened, 2) book meetings, 3) send follow-ups, 4) decide who to write to, 5) draft the first version.
- Why targeting sits fourth: better targeting only pays once you can act on it. A team that can't follow up reliably gains nothing from a perfect list, because the leads leak out through the same hole. "Steps one to three build the container. Step four fills it."

chunks.heading: Steps 1 and 2: logging and booking cost nothing and pay back fast
chunks.text:
- **Logging:** connect a calendar and inbox to a CRM so meetings and threads land on the right record untyped. It removes the Friday hour three reps spend reconstructing Tuesday. No prospect sees it, so a mistake costs a tidy-up, not an account. Setup is an afternoon: connect mailbox and calendar, import the deals spreadsheet, skip workflows for now.
- **Booking:** a shared link ends the four-message exchange about Tuesday at three. Romàn calls it the fastest payback on the list. A rep booking six meetings a month saves roughly an hour of scheduling and loses fewer slots to people who cooled off. Setup is about 20 minutes: one meeting type, hours you'll defend, link in the signature.
- Prices he read on vendor pages in August 2026:
  - Attio is free for up to 3 seats.
  - HubSpot's free tools stop at 2 users; Sales Hub Starter is $7 per seat monthly billed yearly, $20 pay-as-you-go.
  - Pipedrive Lite is $14 per seat monthly billed yearly, no free tier.
  - Cal.com is free for one user; Teams is $12 per user monthly billed yearly.
  - Calendly Standard is $12 per seat monthly, $10 prepaid.
- Cal.com Teams (round-robin) is not worth buying until someone actually needs round-robin.

chunks.heading: Step 3: write follow-ups yourself, let the tool handle timing
chunks.text:
- "Most deals die from silence, not rejection." A three-step sequence recovers more conversations than any new channel added this quarter.
- It is the first automation a prospect notices, so the quality bar rises. His rule: "Write them yourself and let the tool handle the timing."
- Deliverability setup before any prospect hears from you:
  - Buy a sending domain kept away from your main one.
  - Set SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
  - Warm the mailbox for two weeks (a day of technical work, then waiting; "you can't skip the waiting").
- Sender pricing he lists: Smartlead Base $39/mo (2,000 active leads, 6,000 sends, unlimited mailboxes and warmup; CRM and API only from Pro at $94). Instantly Growth $47/mo, $37.60 prepaid (1,000 contacts, 5,000 emails; lead database is a separate subscription). Lemlist Email $69/mo per workspace, $55 prepaid; Multichannel returns to per-seat pricing at $109.
- Budget floor for sending: about $39 a month. Free stops at sending because deliverability needs a separate domain and warmup.

chunks.heading: Step 4: work from live buying signals, not a stale list
chunks.text:
- Replace a static export with signals: a funding round, a job change, a hiring page that suddenly wants five sellers.
- Why lists rot: he cites US median job tenure of 3.9 years and 22% of workers with their employer under a year (BLS), so a list built two quarters ago is already wrong about a chunk of it.
- Setup is about half a day to describe the ICP and pick signals.
- Data-tool pricing he lists:
  - Clay: free tier (100 data credits, 500 actions/month), Launch $185/mo or $167 prepaid. Powerful (waterfalls across 100+ providers) but needs someone who enjoys building tables.
  - Apollo Basic: $49/seat/mo yearly or $59 pay-as-you-go; free plan has 900 credits a year. An email costs one credit, a phone number eight.
  - Hunter: free 50 credits/month; Starter $49 or $34 prepaid. It's a verifier more than a list builder, so use it right before sending.
- Gojiberry, his own product, is $99 a month flat for the team, tracking 30+ buying signals across the socials and the web. He is open that it ranks first in his comparison "because it's ours."

chunks.heading: Step 5 and the four things never to automate
chunks.text:
- **Step 5, drafting:** automate it last, and use the AI writer inside the sender you already bought rather than a fifth subscription. Treat output as a first pass: the tool supplies structure and a subject line, you supply the one sentence proving you read something about the company. Setup is about an hour, mostly on the prompt describing how your team sounds.
- **Never automate:**
  - **The reply to a real reply.** Someone answering is the event you paid for. Write back yourself, from your own mailbox, within the day. The second message in a thread is where trust forms or dies.
  - **Objection handling.** An automated answer treats a specific concern as a category and lands as a brush-off; the conversation ends politely and nobody notices.
  - **Pricing and negotiation.** A number sent by software becomes the anchor, and you lose the context you'd have asked about and the room to move.
  - **Anything a bad list would multiply.** Automating before qualifying the list scales the mistake. CAN-SPAM has no B2B exception, with penalties up to $53,088 per violating message. "Volume turns a sloppy list into an expensive one."
- His view of replacement: automation takes the parts of the job nobody wanted (data entry, scheduling messages, remembering day-four follow-ups). Reps still answer replies, handle objections and quote prices, which is where deals turn.

chunks.heading: The "rule of 7" and how many touches to send
chunks.text:
- He calls "a buyer needs around seven contacts" mid-century advertising lore with no study behind it: "folklore with a useful shape."
- The useful version: most sellers stop after one or two messages, so persistence separates those who book meetings from those who conclude outbound doesn't work. Consistency beats the exact count: "Three touches you send every time will beat seven you send when you remember."
- A ceiling applies. A seventh message to someone who never opened the first six reads as a complaint waiting to happen. Set the sequence at three or four touches, then stop and put the account back in the pool.
- Before automating, write the process on one page: how many touches, how many days apart, what happens on a reply, what happens on silence. Otherwise three reps each follow up at their own rhythm and you get three different machines. "An hour with a document saves you a quarter of confused reporting."

chunks.heading: A four-week plan and stack economics for a 3-person team
chunks.text:
- **Week 1:** Attio free plan (covers exactly three seats), connect mailboxes and calendars, import deals. Cost: $0.
- **Week 2:** each rep gets a free Cal.com account with one 30-minute meeting type. Cost: $0.
- **Week 3:** buy Smartlead Base ($39), register a separate sending domain (roughly $12 a year), connect two mailboxes, switch on warmup, touch no prospects for 14 days, and write the three-step sequence while waiting.
- **Week 4:** fix the list before the sequence goes live. Point the sequence at a signal-based list instead of an export. Gojiberry adds $99 after its 7-day trial.
- Total: $138 a month, $46 per seller.
- The by-the-head comparison he gives for the same four jobs: Pipedrive Growth $39, Calendly Standard $10, Lemlist Multichannel $109, Apollo Basic $49, which comes to $621 for three people. The flat stack still costs $138 when a fourth rep joins.
- Billing model matters more than headline price: senders bill by workspace, data tools by head or credit.
- He expects teams to feel the change in week four rather than week one, because that is when targeting lands on top of working plumbing.

chunks.heading: Where automation goes wrong
chunks.text:
- **Sending before warming the domain:** a new domain firing 200 emails on day one lands in spam and stays there. Google asks bulk senders to keep spam complaints under 0.3% (applied since February 2024). Two weeks of warmup on a dedicated domain costs only patience and protects the mailbox you run the company from.
- **Unverified lists:** bounces waste the send and signal to mailbox providers that you don't know who you're writing to. Verify first; Hunter's free 50 credits a month is enough for a small batch.
- **Tools that don't talk:** a sender that can't write back to the CRM turns reps into copy-paste operators. Check whether the CRM integration is included in your plan or gated a tier higher (he notes Smartlead holds CRM and API back on Base).
- **Unwritten process:** see the one-page sequence rule above.
- **Origin of his targeting view:** before Gojiberry, Romàn prospected on the socials for his previous company, Coco.ai. He noticed the accounts that replied were the ones showing a signal that week: a funding round, a new hire, a comment on the right post. He was hunting intent by hand, one tab at a time. A small team has no operations person to maintain a scoring model and no hours to check 200 profiles a week, so he built that part, kept the price flat so headcount stops mattering, and left the reply to a human.
- Customer results he cites: Wispra gets 60% of weekly demos from intent signals; Mindflow saw a +31% reply rate after moving to intent-based outbound; GTE Localize booked 100+ meetings after swapping email blasts for intent-led outreach.
- His honesty note: he has not run a controlled reply-rate test across the 13 tools and won't invent a percentage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A buyer's guide that splits AI sales agents into autonomous (run the whole loop) and assistive (a rep still sends), then compares ten tools and their pricing models. Core lessons: pick the type before the tool, watch what the price meter counts (seat, team, credits), and lead outreach with a real signal rather than volume. It is a vendor post, so claims favor Gojiberry.

chunks.heading: AI sales agents come in two families, and the type matters more than the ranking
chunks.text:
- Romàn says "AI sales agent" covers two different products, and the type decides more than any vendor ranking does.
- **Autonomous agents** run the whole loop with nobody watching. They find leads, write messages, handle replies and book meetings. You set the ICP, positioning and approval rules once, then the agent works through the week.
  - The trade-off is control: "an agent nobody supervises produces volume rather than pipeline."
- **Assistive agents** (copilots) research the account, draft the reply and flag what deserves attention, but "a person still presses send." They sharpen a rep who already has a list and a full calendar. They fill neither.
- Romàn's rule of thumb:
  - A team of 2 to 10 with no list, no traffic and nobody spare to supervise a tool needs an autonomous agent.
  - Reps who already sell well and need better preparation suit an assistive agent (he names Clay and Gong).
  - A chat agent that qualifies inbound visitors only works the traffic you already earned and does not raise visitor numbers.
- He separates an agent from a chatbot: a chatbot waits for a question, while an agent picks the account, writes the message, sends it, reads the reply and moves the record.
- He separates "AI SDR" from "AI agent": AI SDR describes a job, priced against a salary. AI agent describes an architecture that decides and acts on its own. "Every AI SDR counts as an AI agent, and most AI agents do something far narrower."

chunks.heading: Three capabilities that separate a real agent from a sequencer with a chatbot bolted on
chunks.text:
Romàn suggests checking each one against any demo.
- **Prospecting and enrichment:** the agent builds the list from databases, company sites and live signals, not from an export that is stale by Thursday.
  - He cites US median job tenure of 3.9 years, with 22 percent of employees in post under a year (BLS).
  - He cites B2B databases decaying about 2.1 percent a month (HubSpot), close to a quarter of a list per year.
- **Multi-channel outreach:** email, socials, SMS, WhatsApp and calls, with conversation history following the prospect.
  - "The channel count matters less than the reason for writing, and it isn't close."
  - Volume without targeting leads to blocked domains. Google holds bulk senders to a spam complaint rate below 0.3 percent.
- **Qualification:** the agent answers prospect questions from your documentation, scores the thread against your playbook and routes what clears the bar.
  - An assistive agent shows you the score. An autonomous one acts on it.

chunks.heading: Price grid for ten AI sales agents (August 2026)
chunks.text:
Romàn checked each vendor's pricing page in August 2026. The spread runs from 99 dollars a month to more than 45,000 dollars a year for products that describe themselves in nearly identical words.
- **Gojiberry:** 99 dollars a month for the whole team (2 AI agents, 1,800 prospects contacted). It is monthly with no commitment, and a free plan exists.
- **Artisan:** no published price. Third-party write-ups put annual contracts around 50,000 dollars.
- **11x:** Growth starts at 3,750 dollars a month billed annually (up to 5 end users, 2,000 new prospects). The FAQ quotes 36,000 a year, so ask which applies. Billing is per lead.
- **AiSDR:** publishes every tier. Solo is 250 dollars a month for 200 researched contacts, Explore 900 for 800, Scale 2,500 for 2,500. Only Solo is contract-free. The others want a quarter up front. Unlimited users from the middle tier up.
- **Alta:** no public grid. The Salesforce AppExchange showed a Starter tier at 1,250 dollars per company per month.
- **Topo:** no grid. Third-party listings report 69 euros per user per month, unconfirmed on the vendor page.
- **Clay:** Launch is 185 dollars a month (167 annual) with 2,500 Data Credits and 15,000 Actions. Growth is 495. Seats are unlimited.
- **Apollo:** Basic is 49 dollars per user per month annual (59 monthly). Professional is 79, Organization 119 with a three-seat minimum. Credits move the rest.
- **Gong and Cognism:** no published price. Both are annual platform fee plus per-seat licenses.

chunks.heading: How to read the price: the three variables behind the invoice
chunks.text:
Romàn says the headline number hides three things that set the real bill.
- **Per seat or per team:** a 49 dollar seat costs 147 a month for three reps and 490 for ten. A flat team price doesn't move.
- **Data bundled or billed apart:** Apollo and Artisan include contacts. Gong and Clay assume you bought data elsewhere.
- **Monthly, quarterly or annual billing:** he cites AnyBiz at 497 dollars a month on a quarterly rhythm, which asks for 1,491 before a first meeting is booked.
- Worked example for a team of three:
  - Apollo Basic costs 147 dollars a month on annual billing, or 1,764 dollars a year, before any credit top-ups.
  - Gojiberry costs 99 a month, or 1,188 a year, because the price covers the team.
  - 11x Growth starts at 45,000 dollars a year.
- Budget advice: a team with a few hundred dollars a month and three people should pick on arithmetic. A flat team price beats every per-seat tool, which triples before you start.
- On free tiers: "No meaningful free tier exists in this category." Treat a free plan as a way to see the interface and data quality on your own market. Once you send at volume, you are on a paid plan.
- Fit for small teams: most of the category prices for twenty people. "Two people can run an autonomous agent well, and they can't run a configuration project."

chunks.heading: Choosing by situation
chunks.text:
Romàn's decision guide:
- **Need pipeline and nobody has time to build lists:** autonomous. The list is the bottleneck, and "a copilot sharpens a list you haven't got yet."
- **Reps sell well and need better preparation:** assistive (Clay for the research layer, Gong to read calls back). Neither adds names to the top of the funnel.
- **Want the machine to handle inbound enquiries:** an inbound qualification agent. It sits beside an outbound tool and does not compete for the same budget line.
- **Want to approve every message before it goes:** assistive by default, because full autonomy defeats that point. An approval step can also be added to an autonomous tool.
- **Have a RevOps person and a real budget:** Alta or Artisan, which reward teams that can put hours into configuration.
- **Budget is a few hundred a month and team of three:** a flat team price.
- Vendor-specific takes:
  - Clay: "Building is where it costs you. Fill rate is where it pays you back." Nothing runs until somebody designs it.
  - Apollo: one invoice instead of three is the argument for it, and the credit meter is the argument against.
  - Gong: sharp for a team that already talks to enough people, but it does nothing for the half that finds them.
  - Cognism: the annual contract ends it for most teams of two to ten. Phone-verified mobiles and EMEA coverage are why teams pay for it.

chunks.heading: Do AI sales agents work? Evidence and limits
chunks.text:
- Romàn's verdict: "AI saves real time and it doesn't replace your sales team." They replace the repetitive half of an SDR job (list building, research, first drafts) and leave judgment to you. You set the ICP, approve positioning and take the call.
- No independent body audits reply rates in this market, and nobody has run one identical list through ten agents. He did not run a controlled test and says an invented percentage would tell you less than admitting that. Treat vendor figures as customer stories, not benchmarks, and ask for the sample size.
- Gojiberry customer results he cites:
  - Wispra rebuilt outbound around intent signals and now sources 60 percent of its weekly demos that way.
  - Mindflow wrote only to accounts that had moved and lifted its reply rate by 31 percent.
  - GTE Localize shifted from volume email to intent-driven outreach and passed 100 meetings booked.
  - Baur Software doubled its network without losing the personal tone.
- Limit of signal-based outreach: a signal engine reads what a market leaves behind (job changes, funding, hires, posts, competitor interactions). "When your buyers leave no trace online, no signal engine invents activity that isn't there." Rural contractors who never post, public bodies, or a market of about forty known companies gain little from an intent layer.
- Phone calls: some agents make them. 11x sells Julian for the phone, Alta's Alex handles AI voice conversations, Artisan offers a dialer add-on that briefs a human before the call. Check whether the voice agent talks to the prospect or only prepares your rep.

chunks.heading: Why Romàn built Gojiberry around signals, and what it does
chunks.text:
- Before Gojiberry he ran Coco.ai and spent his days prospecting on socials. He noticed the people who replied were never the ones on any list. They had just changed jobs, posted about a problem, or started following a competitor.
- He chased those signals one browser tab at a time. It worked but "stopped scaling around thirty accounts." Past that, the reason for writing collapses first, and a month later you are running mass outreach with a first-name variable. Hence Gojiberry "starts from the signal rather than from a database."
- What a team of two to ten needs: "neither an AI employee priced against a salary nor a canvas to build one on." It needs the list to arrive already sorted, at a price that doesn't move when the third rep joins.
- How Gojiberry works:
  - Two AI agents. The first watches more than 30 buying signals (job changes, funding rounds, hiring, competitor engagement). The second writes to whatever clears your ICP filter, with the signal attached as the reason for writing.
  - ICP filtering comes first, so nothing unwanted reaches the inbox.
  - Email waterfall across 15+ providers, with contact data included in the plan.
  - Pro is 99 dollars a month for the whole team, 1,800 prospects contacted, no annual contract and no RevOps person required.
- Where he says it fits less well: markets that leave no traces online, and teams whose reps already have a full list and only need preparation help.
